speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 in connection with the first national conference of citizens of Canada representing 27 Solidarity support committees who met in their first national conference on April 24 and 25 at Toronto. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) and the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankow-ski):
That this House resolves, since both the Canadian and Polish governments signed the Helsinki Accord, the Canadian government is morally and legally obliged to defend human rights now suspended in Poland; moreover, that the Canadian ambassador to the United Nations raise the issue of Poland at the United Nations debates; that the Canadian government, using moneys put away for Poland, finance a national or international delegation of accountability to verify whether indeed Canadian food exports to Poland are reaching the people; and finally, that the Canadian government replace the present symbolic and ineffective sanctions with more meaningful ones and therefore implement a full range of trade, diplomatic and cultural sanctions against Poland and the Soviet Bloc until the state of war is lifted in Poland and human, citizen and trade union rights are reinstated.

Madam Speaker, the lack of Liberal leadership in most areas and the lousy Liberal leadership when it was exercised have caused economic disaster throughout this country. Witness only the bungled budget, the disastrous and devastating results of the National Energy Program, and the crippling burden of high interest rates. Now we have yet another victim of Liberal mismanagement. This month tens of thousands of young Canadian students will not be able to find summer employment. It is expected that the student unemployment rate will be 18 per cent to 20 per cent. This means that next fall their further education will be in jeopardy. Since this Liberal government threatens to ruin a whole generation of young Canadians who are the future leaders of the country, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor):
That this House condemn the Liberal government, and in particular the Minister of Employment and Immigration, for the refusal to institute adequate federal programs to enable students to find jobs.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In a

May 17, 1982
speech at Notre Dame University in the United States yesterday, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in effect came out in favour of a nuclear arms freeze by both super powers and a nofirst-use of nuclear weapons pledge, two recommendations found in the recent minority report on security and disarmament. The Prime Minister said:
Let us pledge that we will not be the one to start a war. We are worried by statements in the United States about... first-strike scenarios.
The text of the Prime Minister's speech also said that the United States has persistently taken the qualitative lead in the arms race while the U.S.S.R. tries to catch up, suggesting that the time may indeed be right for a nuclear arms freeze. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie):
That this House, in light of the Prime Minister's remarks, endorse the minority report on security and disarmament and urge the Prime Minister to take the recommendations of that report to UNSSOD II next month in New York, calling specifically for a nuclear weapons freeze and a no-first-use pledge.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, senior citizens, like all those on fixed incomes, are changing their priorities, as instructed by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), by cutting down on their food. They have to pay for their lodging. They have to pay the increased costs of
utilities made high by the federal excise tax and the federal Canadian ownership tax, or their light and power will be cut off. The only priority left to them is to eat less. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley (Mr. McCuish):
That this House urges the government to eliminate the excise tax and Canadian ownership tax or increase the pensions of the people who toiled and sacrificed all of their working years to build this country. They should not have to spend their sunset years "cold" and "hungry."

Therefore I move:
That this House reaffirm its commitment to serious negotiations with native leaders and requests that the federal government provide adequate funding to major native groups, including representatives of native women, so that they may be able to prepare their positions in advance of the constitutional conference.

subsubtopic: LAY-OFFS AFFECTING 55 TO 65 AGE GROUP-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the current economic recession, with its increasing number of layoffs, is hitting hard at Canadians in the 55 to 65-year old bracket. Many are already victims of lay-offs. They are without jobs, often without pensions, and literally without income. And, most of all, they have extremely great difficulty getting back into the labour force. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald):
That the federal government recognize that its economic policies are forcing many Canadians in the 55-65 age group onto the unemployment rolls, and that special attention be given to their particular problems so that they can again become productive members of the labour force.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. speechtext: Madam Speaker, I wonder whether the minister is speaking to two members of his cabinet as well as Messrs. Parizeau and Ryan.

Madam Speaker, since last fall the number of people unemployed in this country has increased by about 150,000. Interest rates are about the same but are starting to rise again. About 5,000 companies have gone bankrupt since the minister's budget of last fall. Thousands of Canadians are concerned about their jobs and concerned about losing their businesses. Will the Minister of Finance explain why he is persisting with a combination of policies which, as he indicated in Europe last week, have brought the economy to its knees? And I might add we are expecting there will be further trouble ahead with these same policies.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if the hon. member were correct in stating that the policies which were being followed by the Government of Canada had brought about the recession in this country and the recession in every industrialized country, then indeed he would be cutting quite a swath. But, of course, the budget and economic policies we are following are directed to trying to bring this economy and to help bring other economies out of the recession in which they presently find themselves.
I might say that there was a very broad consensus at the meetings of the OECD and the interim committee of the International Monetary Fund, made up of finance ministers from all the representative countries, that the mix of policies being followed in Canada was appropriate to the circumstances.

QUERY RESPECTING POSSIBLE CHANGES IN BUDGET LEGISLATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as I have pointed out on many occasions in the past, that there are things which can be done here in Canada, and there are things which the Minister of Finance just totally refuses to do. We saw examples of things which can be done in the Ontario budget of last week. The Ontario budget has turned around. That budget said that three principal elements of this minister's budget will not be adopted by Ontario, principally the change in the capital cost allowance which has such an impact on the creation of jobs and more investment in this country. Is the Minister of Finance considering changes when he brings down the draft legislation for his budget, particularly as it relates to those three areas the Ontario Treasurer saw fit to change in his budget?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member must know that over the past several months we have announced a series of programs intended to help the unemployed. The Minister of Employment and Immigration on several occasions has announced improvements and extensions of existing programs, as well as new programs. The minister in charge of housing has done the same thing through various housing initiatives intended to increase employment in the country. That is the policy of the government-to do everything possible within its means to help those who are unemployed.
I would remind the hon. member that it was not necessary for me to go to Paris to find out about unemployment. If she had been in the House, and I think she was, the Friday before the OECD meetings, she would remember that I did discuss employment during question period and expressed my view that the unemployment figures were disturbingly high. They are very high in Canada, and equally high in the United States. Unemployment figures in all OECD countries are likely to rise to about 30 million by the end of this year. Never, since before the war, have we had unemployment in every country in the world as high as we have at the present time. It is our job, working together, to try to bring solutions to this problem of recession which exists in Canada and every other country in the world.

Madam Speaker, 1 appreciate the minister's genuine concern about unemployment in the United
May 17, 1982

States and in France. I would appreciate it even more if he would turn his attention to the problems of this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary question. Before the minister's budget was brought down, the unemployment figures jumped from 7 per cent to 8 per cent. This should have given the minister some warning last autumn about the seriousness of the unemployment situation. Since the budget has been brought down, unemployment in this country is running close to 10 per cent. It has taken post-war record high unemployment to make the minister realize that it is a problem.
What is it going to take, in the way of additional numbers of people of the unemployment rolls and additional numbers of people without jobs in this country, to make the minister realize there has to be a solution right here in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I obviously cannot agree with the rather naive position taken by the hon. member in her question. She ought to know that many of the depressed industries and many of the declining job opportunities in Canada are due to recession in other countries of the world. It would be rather foolish for Canada to concentrate solely upon its own economy without making recommendations and suggestions about what ought to happen elsewhere.
One clear message came out of the discussions, both in Paris and Helsinki, and that is that the surest way to assist the process of recovery, not only in Canada but in the United States and other European countries, would be some success in bringing down interest rates in the United States. That is a clear message.
The hon. member is talking about what policies ought to be pursued. Can she tell us what policies were adopted at the spectacle in Toronto at the weekend, to help Canada out of the recession?
Get rid of the minister.
That is the best economic policy there is.

subtopic: EXPORT OF NATURAL GAS-CHANGE IN NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD FORMULA
EXPORT OF NATURAL GAS-CHANGE IN NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD FORMULA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, and deals with energy security for Canada. When the Conservative government authorized new exports of natural gas in
Oral Questions
1979, the minister, the then Liberal energy critic, had this to say:
We should be extremely careful and cautious when we talk about exports. We should think in terms of the necessity of conserving it for future generations and of the future needs of our country. The worst thing we could do-
He went on:
-is to export gas for a fast buck or in order to support a faltering dollar.
In view of that concern expressed by the minister when he was in opposition, why is he now reversing himself and supporting the National Energy Board decision to change its formula for needed Canadian reserves to include unproved or trend reserves in order to justify additional gas exports?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: EXPORT OF NATURAL GAS-CHANGE IN NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD FORMULA
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I indeed stand by what I said at that time, and which the hon. member has quoted. The reason I endorsed the conclusion of the National Energy Board is very simply that in the last couple of years Canada has seen a very significant increase in its gas reserves and is now in a better position than it ever was, not only in terms of ensuring a supply of natural gas for domestic needs for more than 25 years in the future, but we can still make good money, and help our economy and our balance of payments by exporting what is surplus to our needs. That is also in the national interest.

subtopic: EXPORT OF NATURAL GAS-CHANGE IN NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD FORMULA
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the minister may have disastrously bad policies, but he is not a fool. He did not answer the question I asked.

Madam Speaker, I asked about a change in the formula. I am not talking about the export of temporary surpluses of gas, I am talking about the fundamental problem which led a former minister, Joe Greene, back in 1971 to accept unproved reserves as the basis of a formula for ascertaining our needs. Considering that under that formula exports were allowed to increase, which led shortly thereafter to a shortfall and the NEB to change its definition so as not to include unproved reserves, why is the government now changing the formula? Is it not precisely because it is after a quick fix to deal with the dollar problem?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have to tell my hon. friend no, that is not the reason. We are in a situation now where, because of the slowdown in the American economy in particular, there is less demand for the authorized exports than we had expected. The demand is only about 60 per cent of production at present. In light of large additional discoveries of gas in Canada in the last couple of years, the NEB has come to the conclusion that we are now in a position to authorize more exports than had been anticipated, that we can be more flexible than we have been. As to what that surplus might be and which companies would be authorized to export it, the NEB will determine that at a later stage.

May 17, 1982
Oral Questions
There has not been one extra metre of gas exported, nor will there be, just because of the NEB decision last week. The NEB has to hold hearings on the various applications before it, and then, on the basis of the modification it has made to the formula, decide how much of a surplus is available for export-after carefully allowing for all the needs of Canadians, as I said, for at least 25 years. I think that is a pretty responsible attitude on the part of the board.
Madam Speaker, the minister looked a little uncertain about his answer, as well he should, because again, for the second time in a row, he did not answer the question.

Madam Speaker, as the minister knows, a few years ago a former minister assured us we had a 900-year supply of gas because he was acting on a formula based on unproved reserves. subsubtopic: POLAND-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE FURTHER MEASURES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. On February 23 the government announced its response to the situation in Poland. It consisted of mild and very ineffective measures against Poland and the U.S.S.R. For example, we suspended academic exchanges and restricted the Polish airline to two flights per week to Canada. In its press release, the Canadian government urged the Polish government to re-establish civil liberties, to end martial law, to release those arrested and restore dialogue with the church and Solidarity. Now three months later, the Prime Minister knows that none of those things have taken place in Poland. Repression is worse than ever. 1. (a) and (b) Canada recently approved an allocation of $106 million as bilateral development assistance for the countries of Central America. He said: Madam Speaker, in many ways it is a historic moment to reach third reading of the young offenders bill which has been on the national agenda for active consideration for nearly two decades.
I want to thank all of the members who contributed to the improvement of the bill in the committee. I must say I liked it the way it went in, but I cannot help but feel that many of the amendments which were put forward and forcefully debated from all sides improved the bill. We have made substantial progress in the criminal justice system in our country in bringing the bill to this point.
I would like to say one word not about a specific subject in the bill, but about the process of meaningful consultation. Even at this moment there are groups, interests and some provincial governments who feel that the bill might benefit from more meaningful consultation. I would like to say to all of them from this place that you reach a time when Parliament has to take its responsibility, and this is that time. As with any difficult decisions we have had to make, there have been, if 1 can put it in vernacular terms, winners and losers. Those who in the consultation process found that their position was not being adopted by their colleagues and other participants in the criminal justice constituency inevitably tend to feel that something would be gained by further consultation, especially if meaningful.
One would not like to argue that absolutely nothing would be attained by further consultation. However, I think hon. members can feel that very little further consensus would be reached by allowing further consultation. If in the process of legislation there was ever a time reached, after 14 years of consultation, when Parliament had to take its responsibility, make the tough decisions and put forward the new young offenders regime, this is the time.
In closing, I want to thank the members on my side for their forbearance in permitting and encouraging the process, and members opposite for their contribution and indeed the forbearance which at this point makes it very likely that the bill will pass third reading today.

Mr. Speaker, the House will be relieved to know that I do not intend to speak at great length. Following the conciliatory remarks and attitude of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan), I want to assure him and the House on behalf of this group that there will not be a long list of speakers. We do not intend at this stage to hold up further passage of this bill.
Indeed, it has been our consistent attitude that, basically and fundamentally, the statutes regarding young people who run afoul of the law are sadly in need of reform. This is not necessarily the great step but it is a step along the road to needed reform of the existing statutes.

May 17, 1982
Young Offenders Act
I said a step because we are in fundamental agreement with the improvements to the law respecting young offenders and, of course, the repeal of the existing law. Indeed, when the Clark administration took office in 1979, it found that there had been, at the ministerial level with at least the two preceding solicitors general, an attitude that the passage of reform legislation was not necessarily a matter of top priority.
That attitude was changed by the Clark administration. The young offenders legislation was given top priority. A meeting was convened of all the justice and law officers of the Crown at the provincial and federal levels at which top priority was given to reform of that law. When the present administration took office, I believe that priority continued, and it resulted in the bill before the House today.
We want to see this bill passed. It is not a perfect piece of legislation by any means, but at least it is a reform. And, to our mind, an improvement over what we have had up until now. If there is a division, we certainly intend to vote for it. However, my belief is that a division will not be required on third reading.
The bill still suffers from defects. In our view, the major defect is the provision that a person is a young offender until he or she reaches age 18. We believe that that age should be lowered to 16 and we have said so consistently. We said it in committee, at second reading in this House and we say it now.
Consistency has not always been shown by all the parties in this House regarding this matter. On second reading there was a five-day debate in this House. That was in April and May of 1981. If there had been a clear indication of government policy and government consistency at that time, the official opposition would have been quite content to see a ten-minute debate. A lot of words, a lot of rhetoric, a lot of time has been devoted to the time wasting that goes on in this chamber.
I would like to refer you, Mr. Speaker, to the five days' debate in April and May of 1981 on second reading stage. We clearly indicated on behalf of the Conservative opposition that in the bill presented by the government and by my friend the Solicitor General, the major defect was the provision that the variations in the maximum age for young offenders in Canada, at that time and at the present time, were going to remain. As a matter of fact, on second reading I had the honour of introducing an amendment, a reasoned amendment which was accepted by the Chair. I read from page 9497 of Hansard for May 12, 1981, when I moved, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour):
That all the words after the word "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this House declines to give second reading to Bill C-61, an act respecting young offenders and to repeal the Juvenile Delinquents Act, because the bill rejects the fundamental principle of equal treatment of all persons before the law by specifying that the act will apply to different age groups in different provinces."
We had a five-day debate on that principle that we espoused-a five-day debate, Mr. Speaker. The arguments and the speeches from just about every government member who
spoke before second reading was given denied that principle. Indeed, the Solicitor General himself in introducing the bill, as reported at page 9308 of Hansard of April 15, 1981, said:
Differences exist as to when an individual is or should be considered sufficiently mature to be held responsible and dealt with as an adult. Practically speaking, due to the specialized programs, resources and services which are in place to deal with young offenders, considerable program shifts and adjustments would be required if the maximum age, which is under 18, were to be made uniform.
In other words, the minister came out flatfootedly against our reasoned amendment. Indeed, he managed to bootleg in another small comment later in the debate, as reported at page 9645 of Hansard of May 15, 1981. The minister said:
I would have wished that the provinces would agree to that age_
That age being 18.
-but the financial implications for provinces which now have a lower age are tremendous. It is by and large a burden which the provinces would have to bear almost completely on their own.
In other words, the Solicitor General was arguing that no one could really come up with a consensus on a uniform age, and therefore there was to be no uniform age. He was arguing that the burden imposed on the provinces by a uniform age of 18 would be so great as to destroy the whole concept of uniformity throughout this country.
I will not burden the House with the history of this bill as it passed though its various stages in the House and in committee. I simply want to point out that the House voted on second reading to reject our concept that there be a uniform age.
When the bill came to the committee one of the first acts of the minister was to indicate that yes, there was now to be a uniform age. We all congratulated him on at long last seeing the light. However, he made what is a mammoth blunder in the eyes of most of us and of most of those at the provincial level who have to deal with this very complex matter. I suggest he also made a blunder in the eyes of a great many people in the private sector-those who have to deal with young people who run afoul of the law-by picking the wrong date. That wrong date is still there.
We were concerned enough about it, Mr. Speaker, that in committee an amendment was moved by the members of this party. But, of course, the government majority, as they did previously in the House, voted down our reasoned amendment and voted it down in this House as well.
I do not want to rub the noses of the Liberal members too hard and too long in their past misdeeds and follies regarding this legislation. I merely point out that today obviously we are going to have a speech or two by government members indicating that yes, this is a step along the right road; yes, this is the direction the government should be headed; and yes, this is a wonderful thing that the Liberal government has done, that they are bringing this bill forward for third reading and finally it is going to be passed by this House. I merely want to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the members of the House that there has been a marvellous flip-flop on the part of the minister and the government over this bill.
The debate in the House could have been shortened considerably if the concept we first proposed had been accepted by
May 17, 1982

the government in the first place. The debate in committee could have been shortened considerably again if the government had accepted the principle of 16 as the maximum age. I am fully convinced that before long that age limit will have to be accepted. As I said in the committee, it is a retrograde step to use the age of 18. We are firmly committed on that. But we feel we have made our point, even though we have not been able to convince the minister. Nevertheless the bill does fulfil the long needed demand for reformation in this whole area of the law. Because of that, we are willing to allow it to reach third reading and to be implemented.
The bill is going to take a much longer time to be implemented as a result of the stand of the minister and the government. In the long run there will be very serious defects in the administration of the bill, at the provincial level especially, because of the extremely burdensome and unnecessary costs which will be imposed on the federal treasury as a result of this government's stand. Sooner or later the age of maturity as far as young offenders are concerned will have to be dropped to 16 years. The age should be 16 now.
We are creating an administrative and financial nightmare. There are only two provinces in the country, Quebec and Manitoba, in which 18 is at present the age of maturity. All the other provinces have a lower age. The nightmare will be beyond belief and it will be the result of the minister and the government sticking to the age of 18. As I say, the age of maturity should be reduced to 16. That has been our position all along. It is still our position; but we also want to see this bill passed.

Mr. Speaker, I too rise to speak on the third reading of Bill C-61, the Young Offenders Act. I agree with those who suggested that in many ways this is a historic day.
There have been no changes in substance to the Juvenile Delinquents Act, originally an act of 1908 with some amendments in 1929, since its original enactment in 1908. Of course, a number of attempts to do so were made. A report was prepared by a special committee of the Department of Justice in 1968. Legislation was tabled in 1970-I believe it was Bill C-192-which was heavily criticized at that time as being a criminal code for children.
After that a number of committees examined the various provisions of the Juvenile Delinquents Act. The report on "Young Persons in Conflict With the Law" was in many ways a progressive document and well ahead of its time. It was tabled by the then solicitor general, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), in 1976 and, following that, the solicitor general in the Conservative government, who has just spoken on this legislation, indicated that it was a priority for his government to amend the provisions of the Juvenile Delinquents Act.
The original bill which was tabled in this House did unquestionably contain a number of important advances over the
Young Offenders Act
provisions of the Juvenile Delinquents Act. For example-and I will cite only a few advances in this legislation-there was an end to status offences which, by the way, tended to discriminate particularly against young women who came into conflict with the law. The sweeping offence of being involved in sexual immorality or other similar vices was used overwhelmingly against young women.
The offence of truancy was one which, it was argued quite rightly, should not be contained within the scope of criminal law dealing with young persons.
Indeterminate sentencing, which was permitted under the Juvenile Delinquents Act, has now finally been ended, and provisions with respect to young persons are being brought into line with those for adults.
There are guidelines in the legislation on transfer of young offenders to adult court, and the minimum age has been increased from seven to 12. I do not think many would argue that young people who are seven, eight, nine, ten and 11 years of age should not be dealt with as young criminals but, rather, should be dealt with within the scope of provincial social services legislation.
Perhaps some of the most important advances in this legislation are the clauses of the bill dealing with procedural safeguards for young people at trial. Too often in the paternalistic approach of the youth court-a closed-door, paternalistic approach-the legal rights of young people were overridden. Now, of course, the courtroom will be opened to public scrutiny, and that is as it should be, although the anonymity of the young person will be maintained. The young person who is before the court will have access to legal counsel whether or not the young person is able to pay for legal counsel. Young people will have the right to bail, a right which for too long has been denied them.
There are a number of other significant advances of a procedural nature in this bill. The provisions with respect to dispositions are broad and varied. Again, we welcome the opportunity for juvenile court justices or youth court justices, as they will now be known-to use a variety of sentences which do not involve incarceration; because in many instances when young people have been put into jail the time they have served in jail has in fact been more destructive to them, and ultimately to the community, than another form of disposition. I will come back to this aspect of the bill later on because, as we will see, far too often governments, both provincial and federal, have refused to put adequate resources into the juvenile justice system in our country. While we can establish a legal framework, as we are doing in passing the proposed young offenders act today, unless governments finally get serious about putting money into this area, we will still see far too many young people in conflict with the law, and ultimately we will see these young persons become hardened adult criminals.
While Bill C-61 did contain a number of progressive steps forward, it did, however, contain a number of very serious flaws. In fact, those flaws, in the view of the New Democratic Party, were so serious that at second reading we voted against

May 17, 1982
Young Offenders Act
the bill. Perhaps the most important weakness in the legislation was the failure of the bill to impose a uniform maximum age right across Canada. Both the official opposition and the New Democratic Party agreed that the principle of equality before the law was made a mockery in this bill, which allowed a young person to be dealt with under the provisions of a youth court in some provinces up to the age of 16, in other provinces up to the age of 17 and in Quebec and Manitoba up to the age of 18. We condemned that particular provision, and we felt so strongly about this denial of equal rights for young persons that we voted against the bill at second reading.
The question then came before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, and after the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) was advised by his legal advisers in the Department of Justice that the bill might very well be challenged under the charter of rights as denying equality before the law, the Solicitor General had to make a decision. He accepted that there would be a uniform age, and the question as to what that age should be then arose.
After having carefully considered this question and after having listened to a number of very outstanding witnesses representing a cross-section of the Canadian criminal justice community, we in this party came to the conclusion that that uniform age should be 18. That age was the age which was proposed by the Solicitor General, and I would like to take a minute or two just to explain why it is that we on this side of the House were prepared to support a uniform maximum age of 18.
First, I note that a lower uniform maximum age such as 17 or 16 would effectively seriously weaken the existing programs in the province of Quebec and in the province of Manitoba. In both those provinces young persons are dealt with within the context of the juvenile justice system up until the age of 18, and if we in Parliament were to impose the maximum age of 16 or 17, what we would be telling those provinces is that we are not prepared to accept the validity of their particular schemes for dealing with young persons. We in this party were not prepared to gut, effectively, those important programs which, in many instances, have been very successful in keeping young persons out of the scope of the adult criminal law and within juvenile detention systems and juvenile justice systems for as long as possible.
The second concern we had in approaching this question of a uniform maximum age was that if the age were lowered to 16, or even to 17, effectively what we would be doing in too many instances is dumping young persons into the adult criminal justice system and into adult prisons, and it was our view that young people should be dealt with within the context of the juvenile justice system for as long as possible, recognizing the right of the community to be protected from crimes by young persons. However, if we were to have a uniform maximum age of 16, this would mean that effectively 16-year-olds and 17-year-olds who came into conflict with the law, no matter how minor their offences, would be dealt with as criminals under the provisions of the Criminal Code and imprisoned with adults and, in many cases, imprisoned with hardened adult criminals. We do not believe this is the most desirable way of
rehabilitating young offenders. We believe we should be putting additional resources into the juvenile justice system for as long as possible so as to keep young people out of contact with adult criminals until the age of 18.
There are those who argue that there are some hardened young persons who indeed should be dealt with as adult criminals because they may have a record of a series of violations of the law. To those persons I point out that indeed they can in fact be dealt with under the provisions of the Criminal Code because the proposed young offenders act does continue to allow for the transfer of young persons over the age of 14 to the adult court system. Those young people who, as has been pointed out, in some instances are perhaps hardened to the youth criminal justice system can indeed be transferred and, in a number of instances, already are being transferred to the adult correctional system. However, for the other young people up to the age of 18, hopefully we as a society will be prepared to accept an additional responsibility to put additional resources into that particular system to ensure that to the extent possible these young persons will be kept out of contact with adult criminals. As I say, we believe the age of 18 is acceptable.
However, it should be borne in mind that by increasing the age to 18 a substantial financial burden is being placed upon a number of provinces and territories. In response to a question raised by me in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and also in a speech in the House of Commons, the Solicitor General indicated that, while he is prepared to look at some additional resources in this area, this was a burden that the provincial and territorial governments would have to bear largely on their own.
If this government is serious about improving and humanizing the system of criminal justice for young persons, it has to be prepared to put additional financial resources into the hands of provinces and territories to ensure that the legal framework which is established in the proposed young offenders act delivers a system which indeed will encourage young people to stay out of involvement with the criminal law. If indeed the federal government does not come up with additional resources, the provisions in the bill which provide, for example, for dispositions alternative to incarceration will be redundant.
The provinces will argue that they cannot afford these provisions, and what we will see is an increased number of young persons dumped into jails for children. That is effectively what detention centres are. There should be disposition before an actual court appearance; in other words, diversion away from the criminal justice system. This will not take place unless the federal government is prepared to ensure additional resources are made available both to itself and to the provinces.
Surely we as a society must accept our responsibility to young people and our responsibility for dealing with many of the circumstances which lead young persons to become
May 17, 1982

involved in crime. I will come to this in a few minutes, Mr. Speaker, but first I will deal with some of the other weaknesses of the present legislation as we see them.
I should note that we are now dealing with third reading stage of the legislation. We did not propose any amendments at report stage despite the fact that we would like to have seen improvements to a number of clauses in the bill. We agreed that if the Solicitor General and the government did not propose amendments at report stage either in the House or in the Senate, we would not do so either, much as we would like to see the bill improved.
I will not go over all the areas of the bill that were dealt with in committee but I will emphasize two or three areas where we think the bill should be strengthened. In fact, in our opinion some of those areas contribute to weakening the existing protection of young persons under the Juvenile Delinquents Act.
Instead of providing increased protection for the community and for the rights of young persons in conflict with the law, the existing Juvenile Delinquents Act, enacted in 1908, is being watered down. Clause 7 of the bill allows young people who have been arrested and detained to be locked up with adults. Under the provisions of the Juvenile Delinquents Act as it now stands, young people under the age of 14 cannot be locked up with adults under any circumstances, but the young offenders bill would allow young people of 12 or 13 or older to be locked up with adult prisoners in certain circumstances. Those circumstances include conditions in which adequate resources do not exist in the community.
Clause 7(3)(a) provides that a young person can be locked up with adults if "no place of detention for young persons is available within a reasonable distance". This will ensure that young people in rural communities, young natives in particular and young people in poorer parts of Canada, in some instances will be locked up with hardened adult criminals.
Surely these young persons are presumed to be innocent. What we are saying is that in those parts of the country in which there are not separate facilities for them, they will be locked up with adults. That represents serious denial of their rights. What we are saying in this legislation is that we are goint to take a step backward and subject these young persons who happen to live on a military base in Canada or outside the country to the provisions of the code of service discipline. In many ways this is a relic of the eighteenth or nineteenth century which denies not only the young persons subject to it but all military personnel many of the fundamental rights which other Canadians are entitled to.

Recently the Senate Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Science produced an excellent report entitled "Child at Risk". The committee documented many of the conditions which unquestionably lead young persons to become involved in crime. It is very important that we as a society accept our responsibility to do what we can to eradicate these conditions. I am not going to go through all the conditions so eloquently documented by that committee, but I will note some of them.
Child abuse has been recognized as a very significant factor in the development of violent criminal behaviour in later years. A number of eminent psychiatrists who appeared before the committee noted that violent criminal behaviour is in many instances a direct result of child abuse and neglect in the first three years of life. In the past our society has paid more attention to cruelty to animals than it has to cruelty to children. This does not just involve the beating of young children; it is part of a broad range of characteristics which can include family instability, minor criminal offences, high mobility, unemployment, and general economic and social stress. I have no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that the conclusion of the committee that violence breeds violence is entirely accurate.
The committee noted as well the phenomenon of violence on television and pointed to a study which showed that in ten years of viewing, an average Canadian child would likely have watched the violent destruction of more than 13,400 people. In the United States it has been estimated that a child is exposed to something like 17,000 murders during his formative years.
The committee pointed to a number of other problems which can often lead to young people coming in conflict with the law. This goes right back to the fetus, to conditions during childbirth, problems which can be attributed to children being shunted from foster home to foster home. There is also the fact that in many instances children, particularly in single parent families, are raised in conditions of abject poverty. Surely we as a society must, if we are serious about eradicating crime among young people, finally start to accept our responsibility to deal with the economic conditions which so often lead young people to become involved in crime.
In 1975 the National Council of Welfare published a report which should be required reading for all Members of Parliament entitled "Poor Kids". I only wish I had the time to read the whole report to Parliament and the people of Canada, but I will just read a couple of extracts from it:
To be born poor is to face a greater likelihood of ill health-in infancy, in childhood and throughout your adult life. To be born poor is to face a lesser likelihood that you will finish high school; lesser still that you will attend university. To be born poor is to face a greater likelihood that you will be judged a delinquent in adolescence and, if so, a greater likelihood that you will be sent to a "correctional institution". When the Solicitor General was a backbencher, he found that to be a good principle. In fact, he did so at the behest of his constituents. Apparently there was a lot of vandalism in his riding. The community organizers came to him and said they needed a back-up to the present law. If parents are irresponsible, the law ought to bring them to account and make them jointly responsible for the children. I think that is good.
That was the view of the Solicitor General when he was a backbencher. A marvellous conversion took place between his move from the back bench to the front bench. When he became a cabinet minister, he either had a conversion or lapse of memory because he felt that it was not an appropriate piece of legislation.
I am quite astounded at that. I think it is a downward move. For support, I have the credo of the Canadian Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children. It underscores this. I quote:
Most parents are willing and able to provide their children with the necessary loving empathic care, given support from others, appropriate understanding of the task and the conviction of its absolute importance.
It is unutterably cruel to permanently maim a human being by failing to provide this quality of care during the first three years of life.
There is an urgency therefore to:
-Re-evaluate all our institutions, traditions and beliefs from this perspective.
-Oppose and weaken all forces which undermine the desire or ability of parents
to successfully carry out a task which ultimately affects us all.
-Support and strengthen all aspects of family and community life which assist parents to meet their obligation to each new member of the human race.
That is a very positive statement. It addresses the perception in the way it ought to be seen-that the family comes first.
Export Development Act
When there are families which are irresponsible, the support mechanisms of the state step in, but only as a final resort.
While we support this legislation and while there are aspects of the bill that are upgrading and do away with some of the anachronisms in the legislation-and it is necessary to do that-there are some very dangerous trends in the legislation.
I want to go on record and absolve myself of the responsibility for those aspects of this legislation that are destructive, and to point out to the members of this House and the Canadian people that there are aspects of this legislation that lead us down the road of statism.
The role of the family is being eroded, the position of the family is being eroded, parental responsibility is being eroded, and there is an easier intrusion on the part of law enforcement agencies, human resource agencies and the court system into the family unit. This will, in effect, allow parents more easily to absolve themselves of their responsibility, allow the state to come in and say to parents that because they are not doing it, the state will have to.
I want to go on record today as one person who tried in this House and in the committee to stop that slide toward a statist trend and intrusion into our family lives, who tried to preserve the integrity and sacredness of the family unit.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ed Lumley (Minister of State (International Trade)) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-l 10, to amend the Export Development Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to initiate second reading debate on Bill C-l 10, to amend the Export Development Corporation Act.
I hope I will have the indulgence of my colleagues since, due to my international travels, this is my first opportunity to speak in this House since becoming a minister, other than answering questions during question period. I would like to speak for a few minutes, before getting into the details of the bill, about the initiatives we have undertaken since March, 1980 with respect to export development, as well as to pay tribute to some of my colleagues in the House.
Most ministers upon entering their portfolios do not have the luxury of having several of their colleagues in the House of

May 17, 1982
Export Development Act
Commons having been their predecessor. For my part, I have four distinguished members of this House who have been previous ministers of trade; the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees), the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson), the hon. member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien) and the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Pepin).
I sincerely appreciate the guidance and counsel of these individual members who have made my job much easier, particularly the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton who has spent a great deal of time working with me. As my neighbouring Member of Parliament he not only has worked hard in his own area of responsibility of transport, but also has spent a great deal of time with me on what I think is his first love, international trade.
1 also want to thank colleagues on both sides of the House who participated in the various trade missions we undertook during the past two years. We decided two years ago that it would be to the advantage of the Canadian business community as well as to all parties in this House to have individual members of Parliament travel with the trade minister to various countries on trade missions with the Canadian business community and participate in those discussions. The contribution made by members on both sides of this House has been applauded by the business community and, I might add, by trade ministers and industry ministers in just about every country that we visited. In particular, I would like to single out my two trade critics, the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) and the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson), who have participated in several trade missions and have made very important contributions to our trade efforts abroad.
Canada is historically a trading nation, depending on international markets to consume close to one-third of the goods and services produce. With respect to goods, almost 50 per cent of domestic production is for the export market.
The degree to which we are successful in selling abroad has a large impact on new investment and new jobs in Canada. Because such a large portion of our GNP is export-oriented, Canada is much more trade dependent on other countries, such as our friends to the south. In addition, because of the relatively small size of Canada's domestic market a successful export effort is crucial, since it provides the opportunity to achieve the economies of scale necessary for Canadian firms to compete effectively at home. All of these factors suggest that the continuous support of Canadian exports is essential.
The ultimate goal, of course, of increased exports is the creation and maintenance of jobs which are consistent with the social and economic goals of Canadians in all regions of our country. It is for this reason that successive governments have recognized the importance of the Export Development Corporation and has supported its efforts.
The international marketplace is becoming increasingly competitive. Developed countries have traditionally stressed exports as the key tool in difficult economic times and as an
engine for economic growth. Competition has always been fierce among these countries and continues to be so today.
Recently the newly industrialized countries, recognizing the validity of economic arguments in favour of increased exports, are putting considerable effort into the development of export markets for their own goods and services. In order to be successful in international markets, Canada must appreciate the challenges of international competition, face them squarely and pursue the many opportunities that exist with imagination and aggressiveness.
What are some of the areas, Mr. Speaker, we have been concentrating on during the last couple of years to increase Canada's exports abroad? First we have put increasing emphasis on capital projects. Why have we emphasized capital projects? There are three very simple reasons, Mr. Speaker. First and foremost, the successful acquisition of a capital project by a Canadian company, or by a consortium of Canadian companies, means an increase in the export of Canadian capital goods, the labour-intensive side of our industrial structure.
Secondly, we have tried to accelerate our aggressiveness in the non-traditional trading markets of Canada. It is very interesting, Mr. Speaker, that the areas of indigenous expertise to Canadians such as in energy, power generations, transportation and communications, etc. are also the major capital projects being undertaken by many of the newly industrialized and less developed countries throughout the world. So by acquiring these major capital projects we increase the image of Canadian manufacturers as excellent suppliers of goods and services in the highest technology sectors.
Thirdly, Mr. Speaker, we increase the image in our own country of our fellow Canadian businesses in terms of being successful in acquiring these contracts-to try and spread the good word-and I think this is having substantial success due to the fact that more Canadians than ever before are bidding on major capital projects throughout the world. Perhaps the best indication of our success in this regard, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that in 1981 we acquired more one-hundred million dollar contracts than at any other period of time in our history. As a matter of fact, we acquired more of these contracts in one year than we acquired in all the years previous. I think that is an indication of the aggressiveness, the international marketing ability and the technical capability of Canadian business men and women in a very difficult international marketplace.
How have we done? What have our results been? Canadian trade results are testimony, I think, to our increasing success in the international marketplace. When we consider the adverse economic conditions which we and our trading partners are facing, as well as the intense competition that exists in all export markets, Canada continues to perform impressively. For instance, merchandise exports increased by 17 per cent in 1980 and a further 10 per cent in 1981, outpacing the growth of the GNP in each of these years. Our 1981 trade surplus of $6.5 billion was exceeded only by the surplus of $7.8 billion in the preceding year. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, the most important statistic is that Canada has had 23 successive months of merchandise trade surplus.
May 17, 1982
Hear, hear!

In the areas of manufactured exports, the labour-intensive side and obviously the most important side to us, we are doing much better than many of our critics would lead us to believe. Some 70 per cent of Canada's merchandise exports take the form of semi- and fully manufactured products, a fact which often seems to escape the notice of those who characterize Canada as simply a country rich in natural resources.
The measurement of a trade surplus is based on the value of exports against the value of imports. I suggest that there is another way of looking at our export data which provides us with new insights about our trade performance. Industrial growth and employment show a direct relationship to the volume of output, and thereby to the volume of trade, and are not simply aggregate values in current dollar terms. Over the period 1970 to 1981, the price index of crude materials, as outlined in StatsCan figures, soared to almost five and one-half times its 1971 base, whereas the increase in the price of end products-"inedible", to use StatsCan terminology-is much more modest, having only slightly more than doubled. The result of the greater increase in the price of crude materials has obscured full recognition of the doubling of the physical volume of end product inedible exports between 1970 and 1981.
In citing these figures, I do not want to imply that I am not concerned about the further growth that still remains to be achieved in our export of fully manufactured end products. Rather, I want to highlight the important progress that Canadians have achieved in the production and sale of manufactured goods, and to stress the importance that this government places on the production of these types of products from a socio-economic perspective. Further, 1 would like to emphasize that growth in this sector is an important aspect of current economic development policy.
One of the other areas of priorization for our trade officials during the past few years, Mr. Speaker, is the area of market analysis. Traditionally, and as used many times in this House by speakers on both sides, we state the figure of 70 per cent as representing our total trade with the United States of America. In the last two years this figure has dropped from 70 per cent to approximately 65 per cent to 66 per cent. Thus it can be seen that Canadian businessmen and women are doing their very best to diversify and develop a much broader base from which to export Canadian goods and services.
In our market analysis we have first of all looked at the areas of the world which would have the largest GNP growth. The 7, 8 and 9 per cent annual GNP growth that used to be experienced by the developed world is now being experienced by countries in the Middle East, the Pacific Rim and in Latin America. During the past two years our officials have been working on special market analysis programs not only for these regions but for specific countries in these regions. The first three of these studies have been made public and I understand from the business community have been very well received.
What have we done with respect to some of the other programs to encourage Canadian business to export? Perhaps
Export Development Act
the most important program incentive to the Canadian business community is the PEMD program, the program for export market development. The Government of Canada last year tripled the budget from the PEMD program. The PEMD program, very simply, Mr. Speaker, is a program to cost-share the risk with Canadian business, particularly small and medium sized businesses, in trying to increase the marketing of their goods and services abroad.
We have opened up a new post in Quito, Ecuador. We will be opening up a new post in Perth, Australia this year and we have under discussion right now a request to cabinet for several other posts which should assist Canadians in markets which we think will improve our ability to export.
On ministerial visits, Mr. Speaker, in the past we have not taken advantage of ministerial visits to a variety of countries as requested by the Canadian business community. During the past two years we have put special drive on furthering ministerial visits to accompany Canadian business people at their request, where and when required. Based on the Canadian Export Association's last annual report, this has indeed been appreciated.
One other point I would like to highlight, one which does not get full credit, relates to the travels of our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The comments of the president of the Canadian Export Association last year at the association's annual convention were indicative of how the Canadian business community appreciates the Prime Minister's travels abroad.
You don't believe that, do you?

The businessmen appreciate the high esteen in which the Prime Minister is held abroad and the doors that are opened to Canadian business by his reputation internationally.
Another positive development is the formation of the Export Trade Development Board which was recommended both by the previous minister in my department and the last time our party was in power. The formation of the Export Trade Development Board has made a very important contribution to a co-ordinated, cohesive approach by the private and public sectors with respect to our trade effort abroad. The only group we were not able to include in the formation of that board were the provincial governments. However, the formations of federal-provincial committees on export promotion and trade policy have given the provinces direct input into the discussions of the Export Trade Development Board and, obviously, into discussions by the Government of Canada with respect to trade policy.
Finally, with respect to new financing programs, which in essence is what we are here to discuss today in relation to Bill C-110, as I have stated repeatedly, the international trading environment is indeed competitive. Among the other things, Canadian exporters face a form of concessionary financing, called credit-mixte, offered by the governments of other industrialized countries. In the face of such competition this government established the EDC credit-mixte program in early 1981. The establishment of this financing instrument was

May 17, 1982
Export Development Act
a measure taken to combat the growth of such financing. While backing Canadian exporters with our own facility as long as necessary, Canada continues to oppose the use of credit-mixte and is working with other like-minded nations to reduce its application.
The firm position which Canada has taken in respect of credit-mixte underlines the position which this government has taken in the broader context of subsidized export financing. Our government has put important efforts into international negotiations to achieve a reduction in the subsidies being offered by some other countries to make the goods and services of their exporters more attractive. I am pleased that important progress has been achieved in this area and particularly that internationally agreed minimum lending rates for official export credits have been adjusted significantly upward in recent weeks. The government is somewhat encouraged by these developments; however, it will continue in its efforts to reduce subsidies in export credits further, allowing Canadians to compete effectively on the basis of price, quality, delivery and service.
Canada is very fortunate to have a strong and internationally oriented banking system. However, the creation for exporters of any country of an acceptable risk environment for trading involves risk management and financing of a nature beyond the capability of their commercial banking and insurance systems. Thus, governments have become involved and act as required to complement facilities offered by the private sector to finance and assume some of the risks associated with export trade.
The Export Development Corporation, the instrument through which official export credit and credit insurance is delivered in Canada, is an integral part of the national trade development policy and program. Continuing government support of the EDC such as that shown in this bill is indicative of the priority which this government places on exports as well as its willingness to help exporters meet international competition.
The EDC is a Crown corporation-not known to the average person in Canada-which provides financial services to Canadian exporters and foreign buyers in order to facilitate and develop export trade. It does this through a wide range of insurance, guarantee and loan services. Because it is a Crown corporation, it enjoys status as a government agency when funding itself and in foreign government dealings. The EDC is determined in its effort to assist Canadian exporters facing tough, government-supported foreign competition while at the same seeking to maintain minimal subsidy levels in the interests of the Canadian taxpayer.
The corporation encourages maximum private sector involvement in the provision of services to exporters, consistent with the realities of international competition. Therefore, an important part of its role is to work in partnership with the
Canadian banking community to combine their efforts effectively to the benefit of the exporter.
The EDC conducts its affairs in accordance with commercial principles and disciplines, seeking, in the long term at least, to cover all costs and preserve the invested capital. Accordingly, it extends its support only to transactions that are in all respects commercially sensible. The corporation is in business to take foreign risks, but it does not insure when, so to speak, the house is on fire; nor would it be prepared to lend to a bankrupt buyer.
The corporation's performance in recent years, particularly in 1981, has been exemplary. I am sure that during this debate individual members will detail the EDC's performance. I will limit my comments to saying that the EDC should be commended for the quality of its operations and particularly for its responsiveness in the last few years to the needs of the exporting community-small and medium-sized in particular-and is deserving of the ongoing parliamentary support which is implicit in this bill.
Bill C-110, which we have before us today, would allow the EDC to continue to fulfil its role in support of Canadian exporters. Three major types of change can be identified. First, the bill extends the corporation's legal capacity to deliver its services. It should be noted that the statutory limits are not an indication of the cost of EDC services to the taxpayer but, rather, represent ceilings on the amount of liabilities which can be incurred by the EDC on behalf of the government. The actual scale of the EDC program is established annually through the government's budgetary systems and necessary appropriations by Parliament.
Second, there are a number of changes which authorize the EDC to improve the range and flexibility of the services it offers to Canadian exporters.
Finally, a third group of amendments is designed to facilitate greater administrative efficiency and speed in the delivery of the corporation's services to the advantage of exporters. I am sure details of the bill will be outlined by colleagues on both sides of the House before the end of this debate.
In summary, I would like to commend the Canadian exporting commmunity for its success in recent years. As I indicated earlier, Canada's trade performance statistics are testimony to the drive and aggressiveness of our exporters in the international marketplace and are indicative of the fact that they are prepared to face the tremendous challenges ahead.
For its part, the government is very active and has undertaken many initiatives recently in the quest to improve further the environment within which Canadian exporters must operate. The amendments proposed in the legislation at hand are a further indication of the continuing support being accorded to exporters by the government through the Export Development Corporation.
May 17, 1982
