It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 40, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assini-boine (Mr. McKenzie)-Veterans Affairs-(a) Request for adjustment increase in pensions, (b) Inquiry respecting date of presentation of legislative amendments; the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn)-The Economy-(a) Level of interest rates, (b) Request that new budget be introduced; the hon. member for Winnipeg-St.James (Mr. Keeper)- Employment-(a) Voluntary affirmative action program- Reported contents of memorandum, (b) Request for introduction of mandatory program.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lumley that Bill C-110, to amend the Export Development Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few comments about Bill C-l 10 but, before doing so, I should like to make a couple of points of a general nature about Canada's trade. In spite of the very glowing picture which has been left with us by the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Lumley), I have to say that I think we in Canada are losing the trade battle. I am afraid that we are going backwards. I know the minister does not like to refer to this and he does not really consider it a valid point, but the fact is that we are losing our share of international trade today and have been for some time. Canada's share of world trade has been on the decline for the last six or seven years, and I think that is a very important point we have to take into account in assessing our trade performance.
The second point is that our deficit in fully manufactured goods in Canada this year will approach $21 billion. That is a very large sum of money. To put it in some sort of perspective, $21 billion is about one third the federal government's level of expenditure for this year. It is about one and one half times the federal government deficit we will be looking at this year. So it is a very significant number. More important is the fact that in order to produce a $6.5 billion surplus in trade we have to have a surplus in our natural resource industries of some $28 billion to offset the deficit in fully manufactured goods of $21 billion.
Export Development Act
While $6.5 billion sounds like a good surplus, Canada is becoming increasingly reliant on its trade surplus for selling the natural resources of coal, iron, natural gas, lumber, forest products, copper, etc. That is another factor we have to take into consideration in our trade performance.
Perhaps the third point that I want to make in connection with trade is the most important. Trade cannot be considered in isolation from all the other things that we do with our customers. Whether we want to believe it or not, we have alienated a good number of our customers over the last few years. Some people do not like to buy from Canada now because of the National Energy Program. They do not want to do business with Canada because of FIRA. They do not want to do business with Canada because we discriminate in some other fashion, be it in fisheries or something else. We certainly do not discriminate against anyone in terms of acid rain.
All these factors have to be taken into account when examining our trade performance and our ability to trade with our neighbours and our customers. We cannot trade in isolation from everything else. When we make a bad friend because we have discriminated by virtue of lower prices and by subsidizing Canadian industry through the National Energy Program, that contravenes the spirit and intent of our agreement under GATT. It is no wonder they get mad at us. The same holds true with FIRA. Some people think we are not playing according to the rules of the game, but then we think some of the people we do business with do not play by the rules of the game either! I like free trade, Mr. Speaker, but I also like fair trade and I think that a good many of the signatories of GATT are not playing the game either.
I come back to the point that trade cannot be considered in isolation from everything else. We have to take a whole political spectrum into account when judging our ability to trade with our customers.
I should like to turn to some of the specific provisions of Bill C-l 10. This bill to amend the Export Development Act essentially increases the limits of borrowing and increases the limits under which the government can undertake to do business in insurance and guarantees. The present legislation allows the Export Development Corporation to take on liabilities equal to ten times the amount of its authorized capital which at present is $1 billion. That means that the government can make loans of up to $10 billion. Up to the present time the EDC has made loans and unfunded commitments totalling almost $8 billion, so it is approaching the upper limit and I can understand that it must be extended. I have no quarrel with giving EDC a greater line of credit to enable it to expand its business. Under the Export Development Act the government was permitted to make loans or to undertake guarantees on its own account as distinct from the Export Development Corporation, up to an amount not to exceed $3.5 billion. Again, the

May 17, 1982
Export Development Act
government is pushing the upper limit so the amount is being raised to $10 billion.
The third element of the legislation is a technical one dealing with the number of directors. The existing legislation allows for 12 directors, of which six must be members of the public service. The amendment to the legislation would raise the number of directors from 12 to 15. Apart from the change in the number of directors, we are dealing with the creation of new financial limits with respect to the Export Development Corporation and the amount that the government is allowed to borrow to finance export sales.
I should now like to deal with the question of financial disclosure, Mr. Speaker. I sense that today there is a lack of trust on the part of the public toward all governments, not least the federal government. I believe the public mistrusts all levels of government, so it is absolutely essential that governments go the extra mile to reveal the financial dealings of all Crown corporations to the public. Not everyone believes in Crown corporations but I happen to believe in the Export Development Corporation. Regardless of whether it is the Export Development Corporation, Petro-Canada or any other Crown corporation, I think it behooves us as parliamentarians to go that extra mile to provide complete financial disclosure. That is what I want to speak about with respect to the Export Development Corporation.
This may become a little complicated, Mr. Speaker, but I shall try to simplify it as much as I can. The money that the Export Development Corporation has loaned out and the commitments it has made amount to close to $10 billion. That is why we need to increase the limit. Of that $10 billion, $4 billion has been borrowed to cover the $8 billion or $10 billion that is committed or loaned. That leaves what we call unfunded disbursements of about $4 billion or $5 billion. In other words, the government has committed Canadians to $5 billion worth of loans that will have to be funded in future at unknown interest rates.
We do not know what the interest rate will be at the time we go to borrow the money but we know what it is today. If the EDC goes into the market today it will have to pay roughly 16 per cent for its money. The Export Development Corporation has made firm commitments to others that it will lend the money at something close to consensus rates. We hope they will be consensus rates, Mr. Speaker.
Another factor is that the government will not say what kind of loans the Export Development Corporation makes. I am not suggesting that the government should tell us the terms of every individual transaction, but it is the Canadian people's money, not the government's, and surely they are entitled to know what the government is committed to on their behalf. But no, the government will not open up, and that is part of the problem. The people do not trust government because government will not put the facts on the table. What the government is saying, in effect, is, "You are not smart enough to know, so we will not tell you."
The government has committed taxpayers to $4 billion or $5 billion in loans at subsidized interest rates for anywhere from 20 to 30 years. But those liabilities have not been funded. We do not know what it is going to cost us at some point down the road, but we do know what it is going to cost us today. What I am driving at here is that the Canadian public should be told what the liability is. For example, if we loan that money out for 15 years at, say, 8 per cent, and we have to borrow at 16 per cent, we are liable for 8 per cent on $5 billion for 15 years. So let us get it up front and tell the Canadian taxpayer what it is really costing. We are increasing the loan limit of the corporation from $10 billion to $20 billion; we are increasing the limit on government account from $3.5 billion to $10 billion; and we are increasing the corporation's authorized capital from $1 billion to $2 billion. Those are pretty big sums of money. The Canadian taxpayer is going to have another $30 billion at risk.
Let us talk about the Candu reactor sales for a moment. They provide a lot of jobs and keep Canada at the forefront of technology. Maybe they are a good thing. I am not convinced that Candus are all that great a thing, but let us assume for a moment that they are. I think the minister confirmed to me in committee that if we sell a Candu to Mexico we could be talking about a $5 billion line of credit. A sale to Roumania, if it goes through, would, I think, be something over $800 million, perhaps $1 billion. I have heard a figure of between $3 billion and $4 billion for the sale to Korea, if it goes through. I am not certain whether we have any commitments there at the moment, but the point is that we could be looking at $10 billion in financing. While I doubt very much that we would be able to sell Candu reactors on the basis of 11 per cent financing, let us assume that we can and that we have to borrow the money today at 16 per cent. We are then talking about a 5 per cent interest spread on $10 billion. That comes out to about $500 million a year.
The point I am getting at is that I think the Canadian people are entitled to know that is the kind of commitment the EDC is making on their behalf. Admittedly, the government does not know what the interest rate is going to be when those loans are actually funded, but let us tell the people, for heaven's sake, what it would cost the taxpayer if we funded those commitments today. No private corporation would ever get past a security exchange without providing that information. You have to tell the people what you are committing them to.
What the government is saying to the public is: We are going to lend all this money out to help Canadian exporters- which is fine-but we do not know what it is going to cost you, the Canadian public. Trust us, we will look after it. We are a good government and you do not have to worry about it.
Well, I think the government has to come back to Parliament. We as parliamentarians are the representatives of the Canadian people, and I think it behooves the government to come to Parliament and say, "Here is what we are committed to." We do not want to be looking over the minister's shoulder on a day to day basis, but when we reach these staggering
May 17, 1982

amounts our priorities could change. The EDC will lose something like $35 million in 1982, and I am not saying that is wrong. As a matter of fact, it may not be enough; perhaps we should be doing more financing at a loss to promote Canadian industry. 1 understand also that it is forecast the EDC will probably lose $60 million in fiscal 1983.
As competition for international trade increases and more and more countries are desperately looking for trade to support their balance of payments, then pressure on all countries to export increases. Who knows what will happen to interest rates? It is very unlikely in the near term that the rates at which we finance Canadian exports will be anything close to the market rates we pay for the funds. I suggest to the minister and to the government that very likely we will be looking at significant interest rate spreads for quite some time. No one knows what is going to happen, but the trends are there. We are facing tough competition to get Canadian goods abroad. We are facing subsidized concessions that our competitors in other countries make. We have to face the fact that our interest rates will remain at a high level. We are looking at a sizeable interest rate spread and at large amounts of money. I do not want the government to come back here looking for a blank cheque. Five per cent, 6 per cent or 10 per cent of $30 billion is a lot of money. 1 do not think the government should have the right to ignore Parliament and just come back to report what commitments it has made. Our priorities could change.
If we should have learned anything in the last year in this Parliament, surely we should have learned that man's ability to forecast is pretty fragile. All we have to do is look back at the National Energy Program and all of the good things that were expected to happen six, seven or eight months ago. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) were saying, "We do not need to make any changes in the National Energy Program; we are still going to get $53 billion over the next five years." I see only two members of cabinet on the opposite side, but I would like to ask them what they think the budget deficit will be or how much oil revenue they think they are going to get now. Some people say the amount received will be $30 billion less than forecast. I do not know what the number is. It might be $30 billion, but let us assume it is $20 billion less. Where will that money come from?
The deficit will be a paltry $13 billion this year. What if the federal deficit reaches $20 billion or $25 billion over the next few years? If that were to happen, would you not think that the government should reconsider its priorities? Does not the government think the Canadian people might want to reconsider what is being spent by the Export Development Corporation? I am not saying that we would cut back on the financing to the Export Development Corporation, but maybe we should reconsider it. Maybe we do not want to commit $10 billion, $15 billion or $20 billion to the sale of Candu reactors subsidized by interest rates of 5 per cent or 6 per cent. Perhaps with
Export Development Act
so many other problems at home, we should be reconsidering our priorities.
I ask the government to amend this legislation so that if it makes a commitment over and above a certain amount in the way of potential losses in the future, it will give us the opportunity as parliamentarians and as representatives of the people to take a look at what it is doing.
I have another point I want to bring to the minister's attention. It is a message I have tried to get across to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) without success for the past three years. It concerns the method of reporting; the question of financial disclosure. I am glad to see the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) is here; I want to get his attention for a moment on this question. I am talking about the estimates. I think the form in which these estimates are presented is a disgrace, not only to the public but to parliamentarians. God help the Canadian public. I happen to be a lowly chartered accountant and I think I can read a few numbers, but I cannot understand the form of this document. I have been in the business for 25 years and I cannot understand the form in which these estimates are presented.
I will not read the amounts but I will read the terminology. There is an item in the 1981 estimates "Program by activities". This is supposed to tell you a whole lot. We find "Export development corporate account: bank so much; Canada account so much; total; less repayments. Corporate account so much; Canada account so much; retained earnings and outside borrowings so much; total estimates."
That is really an informative piece of information which tells everybody absolutely nothing! Surely to goodness we can have a little more information presented than that. We should at least have some form of description which will tell us ordinary parliamentarians what in the world is going on. I do not think that is too much to ask. I ask the minister of state to speak to the President of the Treasury Board to see if something can be done.
What I have just pointed out is typical of so many of the estimates that come before this House. It is typical of the disregard which this government has for people who want to know where the money is going and how it is spent. People want to know the background. It is very difficult even for trained people to understand these estimates. I ask the government again, does it not think it is time to try to put the information in a form which the people of Canada can understand so people can trust their parliamentarians?
My next point deals with the board of directors of this corporation. The number of directors is to be increased from 12 to 15. The present legislation calls for 12 members. If I remember correctly, I believe the present legislation calls for six directors to be public service employees. The export development committee recommended that there be a greater proportion of private sector directors on the board, a recommendation with which I fully concur. In my opinion, any board, public or private, should not consist of a greater number of inside rather than outside directors, because boards must be

Export Development Act
independent. Independence is absolutely critical to the operation of any board, whether public or private. If the directors are under the thumb of a government or are perhaps employees of a corporation, those directors are not in a position to make an independent judgment. My experience, having been in industry over 20 years, leads me to believe that they are not in a position to make an independent judgment. I think it is absolutely wrong for any board of directors to have 50 per cent of its directors being, in effect, inside employees, which is the present situation in the Export Development Corporation.
When the government in its wisdom drafted this piece of legislation, I guess it decided to leave the six public service employees on the board, that it would not do anything to them, but to increase the number to 15. This provided an opportunity to increase the number of private sector representatives on the board but not do anything with the public service employees. The Export Development Corporation does not need 15 directors. It is ridiculous, it is nonsense. EDC is a fairly cut and dried operation and 12 directors is plenty. Let us have nine directors from the private sector who are independent and three directors from the public service. This would be plenty to get the job done.
I have no axe to grind. Obviously the president of the corporation should be a director, but I do not see what useful purpose is served by the Governor of the Bank of Canada being on the board. I am sure he has more important things to do than that at the moment. I do not understand why the president of CIDA should be on the board. I understand that he becomes involved in some of the dealings, but why should he be on the board? I cannot see his being on the board. I certainly cannot see the deputy minister of finance being on the board, or the deputy minister of industry, trade and commerce. The interests of Canadian taxpayers would be far better protected if there were three or four private sector representatives on the board.
I have nothing against these people personally. They are all able and probably capable, but we need independence in that board of directors. Independence is the key to the management of any successful institution, whether it be government or the private sector. I have said that many times in the House, but I do not seem to be able to get my message across. If we do not have independence, all we have is a rubber stamp.
If I invited a person who was working for me to be a member of a board of directors, he would realize that I am his boss and he would not want to say anything against me which might jeopardize his future, salary increases, pension or even security of employment. Therefore, he is not independent. I do not think that all these gentlemen would fall into such a category, but there is a very good chance that they would be yes men rather than representatives acting in the best interests of Canadian taxpayers.
Another matter which I would like to see discussed in committee is the provision of greater opportunity for chartered banks in Canada to participate in export financing. It strikes
me-and I cannot be certain of this without a real in-depth review of the Export Development Corporation-in looking at the financial statements of EDC that the delivery of service is very, very expensive, as is the case with so many things in government. I can think of many reasons why the Export Development Corporation cannot farm out all export financing business to the chartered banking system. It is not an impossibility, but I do not think I agree with that approach because it is necessary for EDC to do certain things with respect to financing, which a chartered bank would not ordinarily do, in the interests of Canadian exports. I hope this matter will be raised in committee, because I think there is opportunity for greater participation on the part of the Canadian banking system than is presently the case.
Perhaps the government could encourage Canadian chartered banks to go further than they are presently by allowing them to look after some of the every day cut and dried export financing and by letting EDC look after special situations. This matter requires a great deal of study. Perhaps we could save a good deal of money in the cost of the administration of EDC but, perhaps even more important, we might be able to limit the amount of funds which EDC and the government will be required to borrow in coming years to finance Canadian exports. We are looking at very substantial sums of money. If we could shift the burden of these borrowings on to the chartered banking system, it would remove an equal amount of burden from the shoulders of Canadian taxpayers, and perhaps we would make EDC a more efficient corporation.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on Bill C-110 which is before the House today. I begin my remarks by responding to the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson) by saying that I am very interested in his ideas on accountability but that I would like to see the wording of the amendments. It would have been interesting to see his party, when it was in power for a short period of time, amend the legislation so that there would have been more accountability.
You made sure that we did not stay there.
We could not do everything in six weeks; we could not clean up the mess in six weeks.

It seems that I have, in a very low key manner, struck a few nerves. I remember that the election took place in May and that Parliament was not recalled until October. There was approximately a five-month break. It was unprecedented that a party which had won an election would take a massive holiday at the expense of the Canadian taxpayers. At any rate, I would be very interested in seeing these amendments because I believe that there should be as much accountability as possible. I believe in openness in government, and I believe that we should reform this institution so that it is more meaningful to us and to the people of Canada. If we can accomplish this in any way, it will make things more open and democratic. I can guarantee that my party and myself are very, very interested.

The hon. member for Calgary South and the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Lumley) have both stressed the importance of trade to our economy. Not many Canadians realize that trade amounts to about 25 per cent of our gross national product. We are one of the great trading nations of the world in terms of depending, for jobs and economic activity, upon the export of our commodities from this country to other parts of the world. Our neighbours to the south, for example, depend upon approximately 12 per cent or 15 per cent of their GNP in terms of trade. Thus, what happens in terms of trade around the world and world economic trends affects Canada more than most other countries. The Export Development Corporation, as we all know, is a Crown corporation which has been set up to facilitate trade and to try to develop trade around the world. It offers such things as insurance to our Canadian exporters. It offers all kinds of financial assistance, credit assistance and export financing to the exporters of Canada. I noticed in the 1981 annual report that a number of very interesting things are happening in relation to export financing. For example, I found that the net earnings of the Export Development Corporation were $2.2 million last year, while two years ago they were some $42 million. I think that this, as the minister indicates, reflects the reality of the trading world today, which is that it is highly competitive, that people from many other countries such as the Japanese, the French, the Germans, the Americans and others, are offering all kinds of highly subsidized rates to their exporters, which puts us in a very difficult position as a nation unless we make a few changes ourselves.
The legislation we have before us today will amend the Export Development Act in about five or six different areas. Many of these areas are very technical, and perhaps we can get into those at the committee stage of the debate, which is to come. Some of them are perhaps a bit more important. We have here, for example, an amendment to increase the size of the board of directors from 12 to 15 people. That is an interesting amendment. I am not sure we need 15 people, but I do like the idea of involving more people who are in the export business. I would also suggest to the minister that since the provinces are so important, perhaps we should involve the provinces a bit more in the spirit of co-operative federalism. Perhaps someone who comes from one of the Crown corporations which exports into the international market should be on the board of directors. We have federal Crown corporations and we have provincial Crown corporations, such as Sask-potash and Hydro-Quebec. Perhaps people from those corporations should be involved.
I also think the time has come in our country when we must start looking at the whole question of economic democracy. When we have a private corporation, a Crown corporation, or a mix of the two, I think it is very important that the employees of a particular company have some representation on the board of directors and some direct input into how that company operates. An employee in the company, be it a
Export Development Act
secretary or working person, is very sensitive as to what that company is doing right or what it is doing wrong. Those are some of the matters we should consider at the committee stage.
There is also an amendment before us which will increase the capitalization of the company from $1 billion to about $2 billion. That reflects the reality of inflation and of the international interest rates. I have already mentioned that we face tremendously stiff competition today from a number of countries, such as France and Japan, when it comes to trade. That is one issue we will have to get around.
I, like the minister and the hon. member for Calgary South, want to mention a few ideas we should be discussing in relation to over-all trade. When we refer to trade, we should not discuss it in isolation. I do not think we should discuss any issue in the world today or in our country in isolation. I suppose, by nature, I am very suspicious of people who go on one issue crusades or one issue campaigns, regardless of the issue, because it should fit into a system of values for Canada and for all of mankind. Therefore, when I refer to trade, I do so in relation to an overall strategy for Canada and how it should fit into the world.
I want to mention about seven or eight different points. The hon. member for Calgary South and the minister himself mentioned the problems we have in exporting fully manufactured goods. In about 1970, we had a trade deficit of around $2.5 billion or $3 billion in fully manufactured goods. Last year, in 1981, our deficit was $21 billion. That meant a lot of money and a lot of jobs which could have been here in Canada or kept here in Canada for Canadian workers. I believe any trade policy and any policy of the EDC must attempt to push the export of fully manufactured products to other parts of the world. That must be part of policy of the Export Development Corporation.
A second point, and I noticed in the annual report that there was a positive trend here last year, is that more and more aid from the Export Development Corporation should go to small business and medium sized enterprises. The multinational corporations and the large companies have a much better chance in terms of their international organization, their economy of scale, their contacts, their internal financing, their long-time establishments and so on, to find the markets, to be able to promote their exports and to finance those exports, than do the ordinary smaller and medium sized enterprises in this country. I also noticed a very interesting statistic which came out of the report of the committee in relation to the National Trading Corporation, which pointed out that some 63 per cent of Canadian businesses knew of the EDC. In other words, about 37 per cent, or over one third of Canadian businesses, were not even aware of the Export Development Corporation. Only 29 per cent of Canadian businesses use the services of the Export Development Corporation. So many people out there who could be exporting something are not aware of the corporation or of its services or, if they are aware, they are not using its services. I have not had the opportunity to sit down and analyse which companies use the corporation's

May 17, 1982
Export Development Act
services and which do not, but my guess would be that the majority of the people who do not are probably those in the small and medium-sized enterprises. If one looks at the nature of our country, one will find that more jobs are created by small and medium-sized businesses and more people work for small and medium-sized businesses than work for the big corporations of Canada. I believe that one of the policies of the EDC should be to make itself known to the small and mediumsized business and to aid them more than it has in the past.
The third point I want to mention, which should fit into our over-all policies, is in relation to the attempt to Canadianize our economy. I know of no other industrialized country in the world which is as controlled by foreign shareholders and companies as is our great nation of Canada. In fact, we find that last year several billion dollars of profit and dividends flowed out of this country to foreign shareholders. The EDC should be trying to promote a policy of Canadianization in terms of making its programs and policies known to Canadian firms. It should perhaps aid and assist some of the Crown corporations a bit more, not only at the federal level but at the provincial level as well. That would be a very important step to take.
A fourth point I might discuss a little more later relates to increased aid to what I would call the sunrise industries, the futuristic industries around the world. By that I mean the industries involved in the whole area of science, high technology and the world of the future. I suppose we are moving into a society where, in a few years, every kid in every classroom will have a computer on his or her desk. It is a very rapidly changing society. There is a massive technological revolution going on out there, so much so that even in our most efficient industries, such as the steel industry, even if there were a booming economy and if we were to get out of the recession, we would probably never gain back all the jobs we had before it started, simply because of technological and scientific change. It is important for our country to ensure that our industries remain competitive and up to date so that as we go through this revolution, we as Canadians will be in the forefront and will control the robots and computers so that they will not control us. That is very important. As I look at the statistics, I find that we are lagging further and further behind in this field. For example, in Japan there are 40 times as many young people attending electrical engineering schools as in Canada, and that means a lack of foresight. In terms of percentage of GNP devoted to research and development, I find that we do not rank equal with Japan, the United States, France or Germany; rather, we are on the level of countries like Ireland, Egypt and Italy.
What's this got to do with the Export Development Corporation?

So when it comes to Canadian trade policy and the EDC, we should be putting more emphasis on developing industries which are involved in the more modern technological side of things. We can do this in areas like communications. The hon. member asks, "What about the EDC?" in terms of Brazil, Canada has signed a contract which will involve some Canadian firms which will supply equipment for
satellites in that country. These are some of the points that should be kept in mind involving the EDC and our trade policy.
A Conservative asked, "What does this have to do with trade?" His party's spokesman mentioned a number of areas for innovation in terms of trade, and so did the minister. I am simply making a few more suggestions myself.
A fifth point, as mentioned by the minister, concerns the need for diversified trade. About two thirds of our trade is with the United States. The Americans are obviously going to be our biggest trading partner. They are our best friend. We are side by side geographically and share a large border with them.
It is very important that we diversify that trade and not put too many eggs in one basket. When the Americans are in trouble and have a recession, we are somewhat isolated and insulated from some of their harsh economic realities. Looking around the world, we should look more and more to the Pacific rim countries, which are very important to British Columbia. We should look to Japan, Latin America, the people's Republic of China, the Middle East and other greatly-populated areas. It is very important that we not rely as much as we do on only one nation for trade.
I have not had a chance to work out all the statistics, but when it comes to the Export Development Corporation, we should be aware of what this does to national policy. Unfortunately, most of our manufacturing and industry is situated in central Canada. Therefore, most of the assistance goes to the corporations located there.
Much of what has been done by DREE, such as equalization payments, for years has been directed to the poorer provinces. The effect of that is diminished or nullified by programs such as those of the Export Development Corporation. It puts money back into that part of Canada that is already more developed and wealthy. It is a very difficult question, but we have to look at EDC in terms of national policy and ensure that what we do to improve underdeveloped provinces is not nullified through the EDC.
My sixth point, and this is very important, is that on the board of directors we have the head of CIDA. It is important that we not forget about world politics. The hon. member from Calgary mentioned world politics; he spoke of our friends and those who are not our friends in terms of our trade policy. We must think of trying to help the Third World and developing nations. There should be a moral and humanitarian purpose to our trade. We should not always be after the big buck and the fast buck but, rather, should try to help those less fortunate than ourselves. We should export some of our knowledge and know-how to help people in other parts of the world become more self-sufficient and thereby improve their standard of living.
When I look at some of the projects financed by the Export Development Corporation, such as the Candu reactor, I am
May 17, 1982

not sure whether those should be our priority. I believe there are other priorities we should be stressing instead.
How would it be financed otherwise?

A member of that hon. member's own party raised some doubts about the Candu reactors about half an hour ago. When we talk about trade and exports, we cannot divorce them from the international political situation. Our role as a more fortunate nation should be to help people in other countries who are less fortunate.
There are a number of other things that one could say. Over the last few months and years we have heard many stories about our being the boy scouts of international trade. In many ways we are. We have to become more aggressive and recognize the realities. We have to diversify our economy and start manufacturing and processing more goods in this country.
One of our problems historically is that we have relied on the exporting of raw materials and importing of finished goods. We export a lot of raw materials that are not processed or refined. This started with Jacques Cartier back in 1608 with the exporting of beaver pelts to Europe and the importing of fur coats. In many ways we still have that kind of simplistic policy, and it has to be changed.
Another problem is that we are afraid to be independent of the United States. We tend to be the shadow of the Americans. We have a tag-along economy, and when they have monetarism in the United States, we in this country tend to follow. The government believes they can squeeze inflation out of the system by upping interest rates and restricting the money supply. Galbraith described this as the horse-and-sparrow system. If you feed enough oats to the horse, perhaps enough oats will pass through for the sparrow. Those policies are not working. I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will put forward new ideas in Versailles when he attends the very important summit to be held there in a few weeks' time.
We have to look at our economic and trade policy and decide where we want to concentrate, look at what we as Canadians do best. Also, we have to look at where Canadians spend their money. When we look at the spending habits of ordinary citizens, we find that between 80 per cent and 85 per cent of the money goes to housing, food and transportation. Because so much of our money goes into those three fields, why not specialize more in those areas? Why not develop those areas more so that we can supply more of our domestic market? When we become better, we can export our technological know-how and products.
I keep watching the clock, Mr. Speaker. I know the time is going on. In concluding, I want to mention five areas where this country can specialize, not only in terms of the domestic market but also of the international market, in areas that are naturals for Canada. I do that because of the rapid changes in the world and the need to modernize our industry to be competitive in world terms. We must do this if we are to continue to provide jobs for Canadians and increase the national pie so
Export Development Act
that we can equalize income, wealth and power in Canada among people and among regions. I will name these five.
First, we must build on our resource base. We have a lot of resources. In the past we have tended to export them as raw materials. Last year we had a $21 billion deficit in manufactured goods. We must, as much as possible, process, manufacture, refine, upgrade and fabricate our natural resources, prior to export.
We have many resources and projects. I think of oil, gas and hydro. Therefore, we use a lot of machinery and equipment. More and more of that machinery and equipment is being imported. Since we use so much of it, it is important that we have an economic strategy to encourage Canadians to produce more of that machinery. Canadians would be put to work producing that machinery for an industry in Canada that will use the machinery.
If we become competitive and produce a quality product, we can export that machinery. I think of Hydro-Quebec and the big hydro projects. We have much expertise there and a potential to produce our own machinery and equipment for the resource sector.
The next thing outside of resources is food and agriculture. I see the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), the minister of agriculture in the Diefenbaker government. He will agree that there must be a greater emphasis on food and agriculture in this country. We are a great food producer and have a small population. We must look at this sector in terms of increasing our exports. The People's Republic of China and other areas could use more Canadian products. In the longer term, they could use more of Canada's knowledge and know-how. This would make other countries self-sufficient in the production of food.
I believe that almost every country can be self-sufficient in the production of food with the proper technology, irrigational and farming skills. I have been to Israel, a small country carved out of the desert. It has become a Garden of Eden in terms of production of food. They export a lot of their products, such as oranges. They do all this despite the fact that they have been faced with many wars over the past 30 years. If it can be done there, it can be done in other countries. We should play our role in terms of exporting the knowledge and technology that we have developed.
We should process more of our foodstuffs as close to the source as possible. This would provide jobs close to the source of production rather than centralizing them in certain parts of the country. We should produce more farm machinery in Canada. That industry has been going downhill. It is now in serious trouble. We have many farm machinery industries that are small but are developing. I can think of three in my own riding of Yorkton-Melville, that is, the Morris Rod-Weeder Company, which has been developed from scratch and is doing very well. I think of Leon's Manufacturing in Yorkton. I think of Ram Industries in Yorkton. These are industries in a small city of 15,000 or 16,000 which have been able to flourish and

Export Development Act
develop. I think we must aid and assist that kind of development across the country. We must also assist as much as possible Co-operative Implements Ltd.
I had a chance a few weeks ago to go to Co-op Implements annual meeting in the town of Preeceville, one of the regions in my riding which gave me an opportunity to understand their concern about the grim and bleak future for farm machinery.
We are an agricultural nation and we should be putting more emphasis on assisting machinery production and everything else that goes into the food and agricultural production for our own markets and for markets overseas and around the world.
Third, Mr. Speaker, there is the question of transportation. We are a big country that stretches for miles. Yet we see smaller countries in size, like the Japanese and the French, who are well able to develop a transportation system. My friend, the hon. member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker) is an ex-railroader and knows more about this than I do. They, the Japanese and French, have a transportation system where the trains travel at 200 kilometres an hour, they are very rapid trains. If those trains were put on our road beds, however, they could not go very far because we do not have the proper road beds. We have a trans-continental train that crawls across the country at a snail's pace in comparison with those high speed trains in other countries. Our trains seem to travel across Canada at only 19 or 20 miles an hour.
We want to keep this country together and develop our expertise. That will give us much knowledge and enable us to increase our exports later on. We should be putting more money and more emphasis on transportation, on rolling stock and on road beds. These things would help not only the prairie farmer but all people right across the country.
This morning I came back from Halifax, where I heard about the problems in SYSCO, a plant where they produce only one commodity, that is, steel for the CNR. If we were to improve our rail beds and our transportation system we could at the same time be putting people to work in Cape Breton Island in producing that steel. We could also be putting people to work in Trenton, Nova Scotia, producing rolling stock to haul our potash and our grain and other products. That would help depressed areas like Cape Breton and give some of those people some hope, and some good feeling about this country.
I have dealt with resources, with food and agriculture, and with transportation, and now I would like to deal with two subjects. One of them is communication. The minister mentioned that we have developed a lot of expertise in communications. I remember being with him in Brazil a few months ago. We were there with Spar, a company that was bidding on a communications payload for a couple of satellites down there in competition with the French. We have not only that company but many other companies, including some federal government Crown corporations and provincial government Crown corporations, such as Saskel in Saskatchewan. They have developed tremendous expertise in communications. We
should build on that. Once again, we are a vast country and we have to develop communications. If we can do it for our market we can become leaders in the world and supply other markets in other continents far, far away.
I would give you one or two examples again . The Saskatchewan Telephone Company decided some time ago that they were going into fibre optics. These are laser beams communications through a little thin glass tube. It is a far more efficient and effective form of communications than the satellite. To get sound from a ground station to a satellite and back again takes about half a second. When you go through the fibre optics, it travels at the speed of light which is almost instantaneous. They decided they were going to develop this sector, and because of that they started shopping around for someone to produce fibre optics. They were able to say to a company like Northern Telecom: "You can get all the contracts for fibre optics in our province, if you come out to Saskatoon and establish a plant." That is what is being done. We have used that kind of leverage to get fibre optics into our province. They have already installed the first fibre optics, which happens to be in my constituency in a rural area, and it is working well. The hope of Saskatchewan Telephones is that after Saskatchewan has been supplied with fibre optics, the plant will become big enough and will be a world leader, because we are now in the forefront of the entire world in this area and we can become a major exporter of fibre optics to other countries around the world. Other countries have not thought of the idea yet, or are just in the embryonic stage of trying to develop fibre optics.
There is also the SED Industries in Saskatoon, a company that is owned half by the university, 25 per cent by the workers at SED, numbering about 300 employees, and 25 per cent by the provincial government. It is high technical industry and it is diversified and develops a lot of products. It produced part of the Canadarm, the space arm for the space shuttle Columbia a few weeks ago. We were able to do that in a small province, in the city of Saskatoon, with a bit of courage and vision and imagination. So I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that with national visage and a national dream, we can do things that are as great and much greater from coast to coast.
The last dimension I should like to mention, Mr. Speaker, is the whole area of high technology. I have referred already to the fact that we are moving into the computer generation, not just into the PacMans and the video games, but into the micro and the silicone chips. It is an area that is revolutionizing very rapidly, where the robots are doing more and more of the calls and where the computers are doing more and more of the work. Everything is going through that massive scientific revolution.
My suggestion is that we will have to put a lot more emphasis on making sure that we are in that race and that we use that technology for ourselves and for a better human life. That technology is going to come. If we do not develop it ourselves explicitly, it will arrive here implicitly through imports, with people demanding cheaper and cheaper imports because they
May 17, 1982

are done through technological change. It is important that we become a leader, it is important that we invest in that kind of future.
I think of a lot of the possibilities that are missed. A friend of mine said, for example, "Why does a province like Ontario, that uses thousands and thousands of word processors, not use some imagination and buy into a computer firm, along with the co-operatives or the unions or anyone else, and establish that firm in an area that has high unemployment and then channel the orders for word processors from departments and industries and the educational systems and the hospitals, to that firm and into that area, to create jobs and economic stimulation in the province of Ontario?" Ontario should do something like that, as Saskatchewan has done in the area of fibre optics and will be doing in fibre optics in the city of Saskatoon.
It is this kind of vision, this kind of future orientation, that we are going to need in terms of a national economic development policy, to keep Canada in the forefront of the twenty-first century.
In conclusion, I emphasize that there are these five areas: resources, food, transportation, communications and technology. I do not think you can deal with anything in isolation in this world. There must be an over-all vision of where we want to go. I suggest that the Export Development Corporation may not be the leader, it may not be able to play a major leadership role, but certainly it can play a player in developing that kind of policy for Canada in the years that lie ahead.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that it is six o'clock. I do not want to indulge the House any longer, except to say to the minister that we will be taking a very serious look in detail at the amendments that are before us, and asking him some questions between now and the final passage of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, in my business career I have had the opportunity to deal with the Export Development Corporation, and that is what prompts me to speak tonight. At First Canadian Place in downtown Toronto a floor of space is devoted to this corporation. It has the finest boardroom I have seen. The boardroom table is three yards across, and the chairs are so comfortable one could fall asleep. Mr. Speaker, you would be very comfortable in one of those boardroom chairs.
The overhead of the Export Development Corporation is something else again, and it is about that I want to speak tonight.
Export Development Act
The Export Development Corporation basically has two functions. The first is its insurance company function. The corporation is designed to insure Canadians who are exporting against the political and economic risks of selling their goods where they may have a difficult time collecting payment for those goods in a lawsuit.
People who export from Canada require some sort of insurance policy which enable them to insure their receivables. The insurance aspect is the first responsibility of the Canadian Export Development Corporation, and I suggest that is the most important responsibility of the corporation.
I am disappointed the minister is not here tonight. I see him coming in now. I am glad he is because I want to repeat that the most important thing the Export Development Corporation does is to provide insurance so that when an exporter sells his goods on commercial terms in a foreign country, he can have credit cleared for the foreign recipient of the goods, and he can be insured against political risks, economic risks, current currency exchange risks and all the risks implicit in selling goods in places where it might not be easy to collect because of political and legal systems. That is the first job of this corporation.
Last year the Export Development Corporation sold insurance for which it received a gross premium of SI4.2 million. As any insurance company does, the EDC invested those premiums and earned investment income of $2.6 million for a total receipt of $16.8 million. It placed reserves against its total collection of $13.6 million, for a profit or a gross margin on its insurance operation of a little over $3 million. Out of its reserves the corporation paid $8.2 million in claims, which was probably the highest payout in history. I think the minister will confirm that. In any event, based on the premiums the corporation charged exporters and based on the income the corporation received from the interest, its gross margin was over $3 million, even allowing $13.6 million as a reserve against claims, and I point out to the House that the corporation paid only $8.2 million out of its reserves. That particular business of the corporation is essential to exports. The exporter has to be able to take his receivable and pledge it to his bank for working capital. Unless the receivable is guaranteed by some sort of insurance policy, the commercial banks in this country do not treat it as worth anything. If a company is involved in exporting, its major problem is being able to borrow against its receivables, so export insurance is probably the most valid thing that this corporation could offer.
For a moment I want to explore with the House the way this insurance corporation handles its concerns because I have been involved in this. I opened a new market in Australia for a company. The Export Development Corporation asked for the status of the people I proposed to sell to. I sent the Export Development Corporation a list of the companies and asked if, in their opinion, they were good credit risks. The corporation replied that it was not their concern to determine that as they

Export Development Act
were only an insurance company, and it was up to me to determine that.
I was absolutely shocked, Mr. Speaker. The corporation took the position that the Canadian manufacturer should supply it with Dun & Bradstreet reports and with other evidence of the quality of the proposed customers. I did that. I went to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce in Sydney and gave it a list of the proposed customers and asked that they be checked. The department did so. It said, this one is pretty good, that one is not very good and so on. Of course I sold to the good ones.
Then I sent the Dun & Bradstreet reports in to the Export Development Corporation. It said, "You sold the goods to those people but you have not got credit approval. We don't like this one or that one, or that Dun & Bradstreet report is not good enough and this one has not got enough capital invested. We will not insure your sales and we want one per cent across the board for our fee, whether we insure them or not."
That particular corporation, which had signed up with the EDC, wound up going private, wound up having to go to Australia and discount Canadian receivables of the merchant bankers through Singapore because the Export Development Corporation, sponsored by the minister, refused to do anything, it was so bureaucratic.
This is the attitude expressed in Toronto in the beautiful boardroom with its nine foot long, three yards wide table and great big comfortable chairs, with its beautiful paintings on the wall-the kind that come from the National Art Gallery. They cannot be sold anywhere else so they are hung in First Canadian Place and people are hung out to dry in First Canadian Place too!
It is about time a bill came before the House that would allow the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs to review the Export Development Corporation, its bureaucracy, its incompetence and its inability to deal with people and make trade move for this country. The corporation is overloaded with people-people who have never met a payroll and who do not know what it is like to go out in the marketplace to try to sell a product. People are told that the Export Development Corporation cannot insure the customer because it has not given approval. The attitude is: cancel the sale or do not make the sale. The Canadian manufacturer has an order, but he must just take his chance. He must take the total political and commercial risk on his own behalf-if his bank will let him-or cancel the order. That is the kind of thing that happens with this corporation day after day after day, Mr. Speaker.
The financial statement of the corporation for this year shows that the gross amount it covered by insurance declined from 1980 to 1981 despite 12 per cent inflation.
I am happy that this bill is before the House, Mr. Speaker, because I want to hear the officers of the corporation and the minister explain why it cannot act sensibly and aggressively; why it cannot make things go for this country.
In its own statement the corporation declares that it has 1,429 people or different companies who have signed contracts for export insurance. The figures produced by the minister in his annual statement show that only some 830 people bothered taking export insurance this year. That is all. Why is that, Mr. Speaker, when export insurance is the most important type of insurance for people who are selling goods abroad? By and large, those goods are financed in the country of purchase and they are sold in the country of purchase. They are manufactured Canadian products sold for consumption in one form or another. Payment is three months or six months, that is all. Large loans are not required, but the Canadian producer needs insurance to make sure the receivable is worth something so that he can pledge it to his bank. He needs a guarantee against the foreign receivable. Without the guarantee he cannot borrow against it, and without borrowing he will not have the cash flow he needs to build the product in the first place. That is what this bill is all about and that is what this corporation is all about.
Saddled with a large bureaucracy and its failure to understand the nuts and bolts of exporting for small business, the corporation has failed badly.
Sir, I want to relate some figures to you. Talk about the Export Development Corporation being an insurance company! Royal Insurance Company took in $470 million in premiums last year. The smallest of the big ten insurance companies, the Fireman's Fund, took in $128 million. It took $14.2 million in premiums; that is where it stands. This is supposed to be a big exporting country, a world trader, and this world trader's insurance company did $14.2 million in premiums and that is all. It does not even rank with an insurance company doing ordinary household policies. Where is the go, the drive, the enthusiasm to sell? We are talking about a Crown corporation with $535 million in capital, $350 million subscribed and $185 million in earned surplus over many years. That is what we are talking about, a company which should be able to do a hell of a lot better-I put that bluntly- than it is doing.
It is only relatively recently, Mr. Speaker, that the company got into the loan business on the international market. That is the reason for the huge increase in authorized capital set out in this bill. It is going to be a big lender. Well, we can see some of the loans it is making and some of the countries it is lending to. Some really secure countries, the Algerias, the Polands. We are supposed to give a government stamp of guarantee on these countries. We should be pretty careful about using the credit of Canada to finance Algeria and Poland. But this minister does not seem to worry about it. No limits are placed on specific countries, the corporation can lend to anyone it wants to, at any time it wants to, up to $20 billion.
This corporation made a total of 115 new loans last year, and has a total of 543 loans outstanding. Strangely enough, the corporation also has 543 employees. Can you imagine, one employee per loan. Of the 115 new loans last year, 13 were to

The minister did not explain that when he explained the bill, but at least he will do so before it gets through the committee stage. Perhaps the president of the EDC will be happy to explain how he can justify 543 employees per 543 loans.
Small business.

My colleague says it is a small business corporation. If you look at the loans, most of them are in packages. You come to Israel and you find there are five loans for computer equipment, all to one company, Control Data Limited. That company is in my riding. Great stuff for Mississauga, but there are five loans. Does it need five employees for five loans to one company? I am happy the EDC and the minister will have to come before the committee to explain why this company has so many employees. How many insurance companies doing $14.2 million in premiums would have 543 employees? How many companies with 543 loans would have 543 employees and offices in Vancouver, Toronto, Ottawa, Montreal and Halifax? They have nine foot wide boardroom tables, big comfy chairs, lots of paintings, and an inch and a half thick broadloom.

Mr. Speaker, we must promote the export of Canadian manufactured products and we must have insurance for those products in order to satisfy banking requirements. We must be prepared to lend the capital required to finance those exports from time to time. But we must do it sensibly and on the basis of value for money paid. The minister talks about the need to export and how essential it is for Canada to be a world trader. However, he must show us that it is being run effectively, efficiently and profitably. It should be run profitably, not in the sense of money at the bottom line necessarily, but profitably for the country. When you wind up with a company which has 543 loans outstanding and 543 employees, one begins to wonder where the efficiency is. Where is the concept of making the country grow and prosper? That is what it is all about. It is not a question of attacking the corporation or the idea, or the reason it might need more capital; it is a question of being concerned with whether we are getting value for money or whether we are being ripped off, as I see it, by ineffective and incompetent management and government which, considering the talent, facilities and money it has behind it, is not doing the kind of things which need to be done in Canada. It is a question of whether we are getting productivity or production for what we are paying; are we getting our money's worth? I say there is grave doubt as to whether this corporation is giving us its money's worth.
I want to point out a couple of things to you about the balance sheet of the company. This year the administration costs for this corporation amounted to $21,410 million. Last year these costs amounted to $15,995 million. The administration costs alone went up 25 per cent in one year. This minister
Export Development Act
was in charge for that year. Can the minister explain to the House why the administration charges of that corporation went up 25 per cent in one year? Can he explain that? The minister might want to say that the problem with the change in profit was interest rates. I want to point out to the minister, from his own statements and nowhere else, that last year, after paying interest on the loan portfolio, he had $39 million left. This year he had $20 million. He lost $19 million in the loan portfolio. When you get down to the bottom line, the profit this year was $2.2 million; last year it was $32 million and the year before it was $42 million. It makes one begin to wonder what has happened. This minister has been in charge of this corporation since 1980. He took over a corporation that showed a bottom line of $42 million. He ran it down to $32 million in one year, and the next year he ran it down to $2.2 million. At that rate he will run it into bankruptcy. Where is this minister's alleged business experience? Where is the bottom line? It is not in the interest differential. I say to you, sir, that it is in the administration costs. The overhead went up $5 million. That is the reason. Did the service to Canadians go up? It did not do so in the insurance portfolio. The gross amount covered by insurance went down. Did it go up in the lending area? Yes, it went up $500 million. That is all it went up, and that is gross assets, about 15 per cent.
One must look at this corporation and its profitability. One must look at whether this corporation is doing the work we have employed it to do. Has this minister, in managing this corporation, done what we have employed him to do? On second reading of this bill, I see there is serious concern whether this corporation is doing what it was engaged to do effectively and profitably. When we take a look at the total number of employees in the corporation, the increase in overhead, the massive decrease in profitability and the massive amount of taxpayers' money in this corporation, we can see that this corporation is not carrying its weight. That is what it is all about. That is why it is important that when this bill goes to committee the minister must be ready to explain in detail his management and his tenure in the office of Minister of State for International Trade. When we were in government, the corporation made a profit of $42 million. During the minister's tenure, he saw when we were in government this profit reduced to $2.2 million. The insurance operation has declined in value. The minister has made loans to the Algerians, the Poles, the Israelis and the Argentinians. What has he really done? He has financed 13 sales for deHavilland Canada Limited. That is a Crown corporation and it, too, is in the hole.
Let us get down to brass tacks. Are we selling Canadian goods? Are we financing Canadian trade? Are we making Canadian trade go? Are we messing around?
This minister knows that the greatest opportunity in trade for Canada is with South Africa and Taiwan. Yet he refuses to open offices in those countries. He refuses to promote trade because he somehow believes it is not politically advantageous for the government to do that. I might agree with his political affiliations if he were Secretary of State for External Affairs

Export Development Act
(Mr. MacGuigan), but he is Minister of State for International Trade. I want to say to the minister that trade knows no boundaries. He had better get into the business of trading and selling for Canada instead of worrying about what the Secretary of State for External Affairs is going to say to the United Church of Canada. I say to the minister, "Let us get on with it." People are buying goods and we ought to be out there selling and winning deals. He has the agency. He has an insurance corporation and he has a finance corporation, and this bill gives him even more power to do that. But he has to get out and do the work. He has to make sure that it is done properly for Canadians. If he cannot do that, then he had better go back to Cornwall, or wherever. We have to make sure that we have somebody in Canada running things that will get trade going again, who will get things moving, who will explore new markets, who will say that Canadian producers and manufacturers are entitled to have sales where sales can be made.
If you want to influence people, you have to influence them by dealing with them. You do not influence people by refusing to deal. You do not influence people by being stupid in your transactions or by saying, "I am a boy scout and I will be fair in my dealings." You influence people by hardnosed dealing.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is a very strong feeling in this country that we have given away our potential. When my friend, the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Jelinek), talks about the unemployment in the automobile industry because of Japanese imports and when people talk about the lack of pork exports to Japan where they pay three times what they pay in Canada for pork, one wonders where the minister has been when it comes to trade. Has he been having a holiday? Has he been having a grand tour around the world? The minister has a lot to answer for regarding the validity of trade in Canada, as well as regarding what he is doing with what he has in the way of an armory to advance, protect, develop and finance new trade for Canadians. With what the minister has in his arsenal, he should be doing a great deal better than he has been doing.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in this debate as one who has had some experience with the current problems faced by the minister. We are looking at a very important area in the economic development of the country. Also it is a very important area when we look at the basic problems in the country today of high unemployment and slow economic growth.
The bill seems to make a number of technical changes as well as some very fundamental financial ones such as the amount of taxpayers' money which the corporation will invest on our behalf.
When I look at the Export Development Corporation, I realize that it is a very positive and important organization. As the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) just said, it is important in the development of exports, both through insurance transactions and capital financing transactions.
Initially in my remarks I want to be quite specific, and then I want to move on to matters of broader concern regarding our over-all trade and economic development policy. In looking at the requests of the minister through these amendments, I must come to the conclusion that he is being irresponsible in the extent of his requests. He is quite aware of what he is doing here. In Clause 5 of the bill he is requesting an increase in the authorized capital from $1 billion to $2 billion or twice the amount of capital which the company has today. What is more important, the company is only using today about one third of its authorized capital or $350 million. He is asking for a blank cheque to go out and do all the things he would like to do without any control by or any further reference to Parliament as to how the funds will be spent. The $350 million supports borrowing of $3.5 billion, and the $2 billion worth of authorized capital supports $20 billion worth of borrowing, which is a full six times the current liabilities of the corporation.
The minister also knows that there is another limitation in the bill which calls for all liabilities of the corporation, for insurance, for capital financing and for other contingent liabilities to be a total of $10 billion. Again the minister is requesting a very substantial increase in the authority. He wants a free hand. I gather this was the minister's first speech as minister in this Parliament, but I do not think he has told the House sufficiently clearly what he wants to use the money for or what are his plans for developing exports for the Canadian marketplace.
We have seen ample evidence in the last couple of years- and more recently some very important mistakes have come to light-of mistakes by the government which have caused Canadian taxpayers a tremendous amount of grief. For example, there are the losses of the Consolidated Computer, a debacle which has seen $125 million written off because of mistakes and lack of control of the government in the operations of a company one step removed from the control of Parliament.
Also the hon. member for Mississauga South referred to the guarantees of a number of Crown corporations. We have seen the government requesting carte blanche authority for a number of Crown corporations. Currently we have before us its request to increase the authorized capital of Petro-Canada from $500 million to $5.5 billion, or ten times its current capital. Again insufficient information has been given to Parliament to allow it to judge whether it is an appropriate decision to make. There are billions of dollars outside the scrutiny of Parliament at the present time. Again referring to the Consolidated Computer mess, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) never asked during his entire period of time in office who caused the problems or which officials reporting to him were responsible for the mistakes or the lack of control that resulted in a $125 million loss. We tried to find out who it was, but the minister said, "No, I will not tell you". Then we said, "Did you ask? Do you know yourself who caused the problems or who was responsible?" No, he did not ask, that was the answer we obtained.
