For that reason we must have a better understanding of the use of these moneys. We cannot forget that it is the money of taxpayers which is at risk here, not just money borrowed out of the air and spent on behalf of taxpayers by the minister and his officials. There will be no further recourse to Parliament. There is no further way to draw information out of the minister or to have some degree of control over the operations of the organization, because any increases will now be done by order in council-the same old way, by order in council. How many times have we heard that there is a rubber stamp from cabinet for the minister to go ahead and spend money?
I have referred to this because that $2 billion will now allow for a substantial increase in borrowings by the corporation to finance its operations. We also know that the corporation is an agent of Her Majesty, therefore the obligations of the Export Development Corporation are the obligations of the government and, therefore, direct obligations of the taxpayers. When we see this vast amount of money being authorized and also understand that there will be considerable financing received from the general public and from foreign investors, we realize that they are all direct obligations of Canadian taxpayers and that as parliamentarians we must take very seriously the authorization of this increase in capitalization.
Let me turn to another area of the operations of the Export Development Corporation which 1 raised with the minister in committee about two or three weeks ago. I am referring to the mandate of the EDC. What is its mandate? Is its mandate to make a profit? Is it to break even, or has some other fuzzier mandate been given to the corporation? With this vast increase in capitalization there are possibilities for a very substantial hidden subsidy, because as the corporation draws down capital funds from the government, if it does not make money and breaks even, people will say that it is good. If the corporation does not lose money or show a loss-and they know that with international competition it is tough to make a profit-people will say that EDC has done well. But we must not forget that the $1,650 million which will be drawn down in capital funds by the corporation must support an interest rate because the money is being borrowed from the markets by the Government of Canada. Thus, there is an indirect subsidy here.
1 think the minister said in committee that he proposed to use an increasing proportion of equity capital funds to support the loan capital as a means of subsidizing indirectly or in a hidden way the exports of Canadians. As hon. members have heard me say on a number of prior occasions, I am in favour of increasing trade and I am in favour of the government doing whatever is reasonable to increase the exports of this country. I believe in trade. It is very important to our wellbeing, both economic and social. But, at the same time, it is essential that any subsidy provided to our exporters in this country is known to taxpayers and to parliamentarians. I do not think we will have nearly the same control if we follow the way proposed by the minister, because it will not be apparent, it will be a hidden subsidy. I can hear the minister now; he will come into this House and say, "We broke even despite the competition from the Japanese, the French, the English and the Germans, and
Export Development Act
that is good." He will not say for one minute that the vast amount of capital he has drawn down from the Consolidated Revenue Fund has not earned a penny. That $2 billion, earning no money, is equivalent to a $200 million a year subsidy at 10 per cent, and a $300 million subsidy at 15 per cent. The point I am making is that we do not have the proper control here.
Let me refer briefly to another element of the annual report which came out after the minister presented himself to the committee a few weeks ago. It concerns the whole question of rescheduled loans, loans which have effectively gone bad but which the government has taken steps to extend, through the Export Development Corporation, so that they do not show up as bad loans in the books. This year there has been an increase of $30 million in these loans, and there is a substantial increase in the provision for bad debts amounting to another $15 million. I think this acknowledges our difficulty in the international trading markets today. It is also a warning sign that because these problems are growing there is a greater degree of risk to the Export Development Corporation. Viewed from that standpoint, it is all the more reason we should not be asked to give carte blanche, a blank cheque, to the minister to go ahead and operate and, through him, to the Export Development Corporation to operate without parliamentary control, without the duty of having to come back to justify a further increase of capital. I must say to Your Honour that in the context of the problems with the Consolidated Computer Corporation, I am not convinced that we should allow ministers opposite the use of the taxpayers' funds in that way. When we were in office, we initiated some studies on the extension of the Export Development operations into the private sector, sharing the operations of EDC with the banking community and others in the private sector who also had expertise in international trading markets. I must say that I am disappointed that we have not seen any extension or any further work done on this privatization, if I can use that word in a broader sense than is normally given it. I believe there has been a considerable increase in the expertise of the private sector since EDC was formed and, prior to that, since the Export Credit Insurance Corporation was formed. These two organization were formed because there was a gap, a void, in the capabilities and in the interests of people in the financial sector to become involved in international trade. But now, in the past few years, there has been a considerable increase in expertise, and most of the loan packages put together by the EDC are put together in consultation and in co-operation with the private sector, so there is a private sector package and participation by the EDC.
I believe there are other ways, more than have been followed to date, of drawing in the expertise and financial resources of the private sector to increase our capacities as a trading nation. It is important that this government initiate a study to this effect, and I call on the minister to do this, to carry forward the work we had started, to discuss the situation with some of

Export Development Act
the banks and other institutions which have an interest here and to consider ways in which they can become involved. I do not believe the small business community is as well served as it could be by the Export Development Corporation.
My colleague, the hon. member for Mississauga South has referred to the size of the EDC staff and the number of loans it has handled over the past year. Elowever, when one looks at the size of these loans, one finds that it points out the nature of the involvement of EDC in that it is more concerned with huge projects. A number of huge projects are on the drawing boards and are being actively pursued by Canadian exporters in cooperation with the EDC and the banking community. However, more than likely, the EDC does not have the time, the staff, nor the interest to ensure that the small business community is as actively served as are the major corporations. It is probably human nature that if one has a $ 100 million here and a $10 million or a $1 million deal over here, one will spend more time with the $100 million deal.
It is for that reason that the government should try to co-opt the resources, the expertise and the day to day business contacts of the banking community to try to service that small business sector more efficiently and more effectively than has been the case to date. So I call on the minister to try to involve the private sector in the decision-making of the corporation to a greater extent and also to take that one step further so that a task force or some form of consultative body might be created with a specific mandate to increase the degree of activity that the private sector can take over from the operations of the Export Development Corporation.
I would like to address the balance of my remarks to a very important area of trade policy, that is, I would like to look behind trade policy to see what we are doing in our economic and industrial development policies. The minister is probably quite aware of the fact that if the proper economic development policies are not in place, he will be spinning his wheels more and more as time goes on. If we are not competitive as a nation, if our inflation rate continues at today's rate of 4 per cent, 5 per cent or 6 per cent, whatever is the proper ratio compared to that of the United States or of our other major competitors, and if our product development is not up to the current standard of technology, he will be spinning his wheels. He will be fighting an ongoing battle, which he is bound to lose.
Looking back over the past ten years, we can see that we have been losing that battle because we have seen our manufacturing trade deficit increase from about $3 billion ten years ago to a current level of about $21 billion or $22 billion. I am sure the minister will say that we still have a positive balance of trade. Last year I believe our trade balance was $5.8 billion. He is very proud of that. The important fact he has to recognize is that during that same year, the manufacturing trade deficit increased from $17 billion to $22 billion. We lost $5 billion in our balance of trade. This essentially means we exported probably 50,000 to 60,000 jobs to other markets in the United States, the Far East, Germany and so on.
Let us dwell for a minute on the importance of our economic development policies. Let me take one by one those policies that we in the Conservative Party feel are essential and must be the yardsticks which the government should build around in order to make the minister's job easier than it is today.
The first is training. If we do not develop the expertise and capability for our people in this country, it makes it very difficult to take advantage of the new technologies that will be coming forward over the next few years. We are not just looking at training of people who are already on the job, but also at training in the high schools, community colleges and universities. We must get the programs together to allow us to have the skilled people available to take advantage of the opportunities that will be ours in the future. That is why we have opposed so strenuously the cuts in post-secondary education funding. It is cutting our future at a time when we need it most.
We also have to look at a much greater degree of cooperation between the federal and provincial governments. I was very disappointed when the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) announced his new policy. Right on the heels of that announcement, not one, not two, but ten provincial ministers spoke out strongly against the initiatives the federal government was taking. Surely something was wrong that there could not have been that degree of cooperation to allow for policies announced at the federal level to be warmly received by the provincial and municipal governments. If we cannot have that co-operation, we will continue to knock our heads against each other and not move ahead in cooperation to fight the problems of not just our Canadian domestic market, but the world market.
The next important point in any economic development strategy has to be research and development. My colleague, the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. Gilchrist), has spoken time and again and has been very specific in recent speeches in the House about moves we can make in this country to improve our capacity to develop our own products for our own markets rather than always buy from outside. We have lost the technological development. We do not get the advantage in terms of the expertise that we gain from developing things on our own. We lose a tremendous amount of profit which can be reinvested into development for further technology-
We have seen this country stumbling along in seventh place of all the industrialized summit nations in research and development over the past seven or eight years. Those figures are right out of the government's document "Economic Development for the Medium Term". From time to time we hear how sad it is to watch the way the Italians and the English struggle along with all their economic problems. Let us look at some figures drawn from that document. Our productivity improvement-

May 17, 1982

That is the point I am going to make. Our productivity improvement has been one seventh the productivity improvement of the United Kingdom and one eleventh of that of the Italians. The government says that we have a commitment, that 1 and one half per cent of our GNP will be invested in research and development. The government has been saying that for four years, yet we continue to stumble behind further and further. We are not reaching that goal because policies have not been put together to allow us to do so.
Time and again this government comes out with the right objectives, but it does not know how to get there. It does not understand the problems. The government does not know how to go about finding the ways to achieve those objectives. That is why I urge government members to listen to the speeches of my colleague from Scarborough East who has done considerable work in developing policies here.
1 would like to say that we can wait until the next election when we can put in those policies ourselves as a government, but we do not have time. People are losing their jobs. We are losing ground day in and day out in the technology race. In the meantime I urge the government to listen to my colleague from Scarborough.
Let us look at some of the broader problems such as inflation. If we cannot get inflation under control in this country, we are going to lose our competitive position. In the mid-1970s when John Turner was at the helm, government spending ran at 26 per cent, 27 per cent and 28 per cent per annum. We had a runaway monetary policy and no control whatsoever over public sector collective bargaining. John Turner was saying at the time that his was the government of restraint, that that was to be the year they would control government spending. That was the year that government spending increased by 26 per cent.
The hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Pepin) saw that from the outside. He had to come back to pick up the pieces as chairman of the anti-inflation board. He understands the problem. Unfortunately, he is not having much impact with the man in the next seat to him who is inviting inflation. Therefore, it still continues to be a major problem, and we are not getting any action.
That is the same government that said this will be the policy of restraint. What happened last year? Government spending went up 22 per cent. What happened to our inflation rate? It went from 9 per cent to 12 per cent. It is no surprise that what happened caused inflation to gQ up.
As I said a minute ago, the government has all the right objectives, but it does not know how to get there. It does not know how to reach those goals. Let us look at another fairly broad program. That is the world product mandate approach to economic development. This is a policy that will be very important for this country to follow in the years ahead.
In this country we have many companies that are subsidiaries of multinationals. That is a fact of life. It is something that developed from loose policies of the Liberal Party in the fifties
Export Development Act
and sixties. It has developed contrary to statements made by that party, but we have that problem.
It is a fact that many foreign companies are represented here. What can we do, kick them all out or make the best use of them here? I say we have to make the best use of them here. One way to do that is to make them more independent from their parent companies, giving them such greater control over their product line and over the operations and development of their company so that we can improve the economy of the country over all. By giving them encouragement to develop the world product mandate, control of their product line from the research stage through production and marketing, having total control of that over-all cycle, we can develop our country better.
People talk about Canadianization. We have a much greater chance of getting more and more Canadian ownership of these companies if we allow that cycle to develop. Once those companies achieve a greater degree of stability and independence and less reliance on their parent company, at that point we will see many more of those companies going to market and being realistic investments for Canadian investors.
Let me move now to the whole question of dumping.
Did you read the Gillespie guidelines?

I have read them. The minister asks, "Have I read the Gillespie guidelines?" I have also asked his colleague, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion and Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce about these Gillespie guidelines. He says yes, but he also has written that no one is paying any attention to them because the government does not pay attention to them themselves.
That is not so at all.
When were the Gillespie guidelines discussed in this House last?
Last year.

He says they were. I draw the minister's attention to the fact that the agenda of Parliament is controlled by the government, not by the opposition. Surely he has been around long enough to know that. These guidelines, if they are to be of any use, have to be implemented by the government.
They are being implemented.

I have yet to hear of any serious attention being paid to them by the government, to the development of the world products, to the development of a greater degree of independence of the subsidiaries of foreign companies in Canada. The only thrust of that government is "kick 'em, get rid of the foreign subsidiaries, tell them to sell out," "get rid of the foreign investment from this country and take the jobs that go with them, too." That is the attitude of the government, and

May 17, 1982
Export Development Act
it does not work. That is why there is one and a quarter million unemployed today.
Oh, oh!

I think the minister has some experience with this. I would encourage him to flex his muscles a bit, if he has not been getting too flabby over the last little while. Let him flex those muscles a little and possibly show the people who are exporting to this country that we are not going to accept dumping here, that we are not going to accept the fact that they are using our markets as a way of supporting jobs back in Japan, jobs in Germany or jobs in Brazil. He should get tougher there and recognize that when a Japanese company sells something here at 10 per cent, 20 per cent, 30 per cent below the prices at home, there is not much we can do. Where can we buy that here? We are exporting jobs to Japan, we are making their life much easier for them and we are increasing our unemployment here.
I encourage the minister to discuss the whole question of dumping to a much greater extent with the people he is trying to fight with, in Japan, because if he says there will be no selling, no sales of electric generators or turbines or other products that we sell in this country, that would make for a much healthier economic and industrial climate.
Let me move to savings and investment, Mr. Speaker. The attitudes to savings and investments are one of the critical problems. We had a budget brought down last November which had the effect of totally undermining the attitudes of entrepreneurs, the attitudes of people who are investing money, of people who are saving money for their retirement. These were moneys that will be reinvested in the economy to provide the wherewithal for the various things I talked about in the last few minutes. The government must learn that you cannot fool around with how people regard their savings, savings that they have worked for years to develop, businesses that they have worked for years to develop, you cannot tamper with that. We have seen the direct result of that tampering in the past couple of years, with the energy program and the attitude toward foreign investment and the attitude towards broader intervention in the economy, and then the budget on top of that.
Last year we had an outflow of capital, domestic capital as well as foreign capital, from this country, totalling some $19 billion. That is a lot of money, Mr. Speaker. It represents one tar sands and half of the Cold Lake plan. It represents about one and a half times the total amount of money that we spend from coast to coast on housing. If that money had been invested in this country it would have created some 200,000 jobs. That is equivalent to all of the people who are unemployed in Toronto, in Hamilton, in London and in Windsor. That is why it is such a serious problem, and it is a serious problem because the government has ignored the impact of their policies on the investment attitude and the savings attitude of the people. People are scared, they are scared that they are going to lose their savings and lose their business, because of the attitudes and policies followed by this Minister
of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) so they are shooting their money out of the country.
People have said, "Let us let the Canadian dollar drop, let the interest rates drop, and then the Canadian dollar will drop." That is okay. It will help the minister sell more exports. But that is a short-term palliative, it is a short-term relief for long-term grief, and it does not work. Once we get the dollar down, what is going to hold it at that level? We will have greater inflation, we will have higher interest rates, we will get the dollar down and have the same high interest rates as we have today. That is the wrong way. It is the wrong way to approach the problem. We have to get the basic economic development policies right.
I say to the minister, do not just throw money at the problem-as he is doing now with the Export Development Corporation, do not throw money at the problem-as he was talking of doing with the national trading corporation that, thank God, has now gone the way of the wild goose. Let us get the economic development policy right, because that is the way he will make his job easier. He has to speak to the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion and Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
We have a great opportunity to build up this country but the policies that we have been following over the past ten years are a burden, and that burden is apparent in the huge increase in the manufacturing trade deficit.
We have to make some changes. That is the positive approach that I am trying to take in the debate tonight, to encourage the minister to take these ideas to his colleagues, to encourage the economic-development thinking of his party, so that we can attack the basic problems that are causing so many difficulties in the country today.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I think the House has been well served tonight by the remarks of several members of the opposition. I am thinking of the member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson) who put forward a policy of approach to the minister. Also, the member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) laid down the priorities of trading in techniques of production. We had the member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) bringing together his considerable experience in the actual question of efficiency of the corporation. We have heard from the member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) speaking about the credit responsibility of the corporation and also about the relationship to the economic growth of the nation.
The minister himself should be congratulated on bringing this bill in, with clause 1 in it, that I will speak on in a minute. Apart from that, he has paid the House great courtesy by coming in and listening. These speakers have been tough, but they have been constructive. The minister is to be congratulated for paying the courtesy of listening to this House, because the only thing he can do is to listen. This is a Parliament, a

May 17, 1982

talking place, and the talking has been of a very high standard tonight.
My remarks will be on one point in the bill and may include a little philosophy. It gives the minister a great opportunity to expand the services of the Export Development Corporation and do so in a way that does not put any extra great bonds on to the ways and means of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). I am talking about the capital structure. This particular corporation is founded on a principle similar to the principle on which the Farm Credit Corporation was founded in 1959. The Farm Credit Corporation has a capital structure and, depending upon how much money is put into that capital, the Farm Credit Corporation can lend up to 25 times as much as that capital. It has one of the characteristics of a bank. The Export Development Corporation has a multiplier of only ten, but it has a bigger capital base. That base is now being raised to $2 billion, and if the multiplier is ten, that is a sizeable sum of money to have to play in the big poker game known as world trade.
What struck me as radical and what struck me as more than important was the amendment contained in Clause 6. I will read it into the record to make certain the record shows there is a consistency here which, for government, is rare indeed. Clause 6 says:
Section 12 of the said act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
I have described the previous section in a general way. Under this amendment the new Section 12 would say:
The Corporation may, with the approval of the Minister of Finance, borrow money by any means, including issuing and selling bonds, debentures, notes and other evidences of indebtedness of the Corporation.
If with that one amendment an aggressive, intelligent group of people working under the minister-and according to the hon. member for Mississauga South there are 543 of them-
One for every loan.

-cannot put together a series of deals and ideas as to how to get money into the corporation much cheaper than they can get it by having to borrow from the Consolidated Revenue Fund, they are not worth their salt.
This same sort of amendment appeared in a previous bill of this session, Bill C-88, regarding the Farm Credit Corporation. I will not read it, but it is exactly the same, word for word, as the amendment we have in this bill.
What to me is so exciting about this is that if I were to put myself into a minister's position and try to do an aggressive, constructive job, I would like nothing better if someone gave me the key to the kingdom. Lawyers in the Department of Justice tell us that the words "by any means" mean what they say, and when I proposed an amendment to this section in the Farm Credit Corporation Act, it was turned down as being unnecessary. I wanted greater certainty, and I named some of
Export Development Act
the other techniques on the ground that the lawyers say that that clause "by any means" means exactly what it says.
What are those other means by which money can be put into the capital account-and therefore into the lending account- of this corporation? One technique which was put forward a year ago in the House by the Conservatives was that we could use the principle of the Small Business Development Bond. That does not mean that we have to call it the Small Business Development Bond. In plain English it means we could use the principle of the Small Business Development Bond, which is well established as a precedent in our Financial history as well as in the financial histories of the United States and other countries. The principle is very simple. If an individual in Canada lends money for any worthwhile national or social purpose, that person does not have to pay tax on his income from that loan. At the time of the First World War we used it for bonds, but the Crosbie budget of 1979 laid it down as a principle to get money into the hands of small business, which included incorporated farms. That principle was a good principle because when the banks began to realize its potential, they began to lend money to small businesses and farmers across Canada at a little above half the normal interest rate. That principle is workable.
The administration or handling of this money could be put into an organization which is free from the difficulties of working with a civil service operation, and I suggest the minister should be asking the people of this corporation to be laying plans down now, long before the bill goes through committee. They should be making plans now to put before the Treasury Board, the Department of Finance and, eventually, the cabinet which will be acceptable to the Department of Finance.
The only argument I have heard against this approach by the Farm Credit Corporation, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation and this export agency is that it may take an amendment to the Income Tax Act. This should be faced up to right away because if the Income Tax Act can be amended for the Small Business Development Bond, it should not be very difficult to get a similar amendment through for these other agencies. I suggest to the minister very seriously that he work in co-operation with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), who has the same clause in his legislation, and see if they cannot put together a proposal which would include this method of raising money cheaply. If they can raise money at half the going interest rate because of the exemption from federal tax, then they have a base for cheap money on which they can begin to build and expand by giving cheaper loans to borrowers. As the minister knows, this is very important in the great fight for markets. We are competing, really, for credit arrangements. We might have the best product in the world, such as the Candu; we might have the best farm machinery in the world, which we have; and we might have the best quality steel at the lowest price in the world, which we have; but we cannot sell unless we offer credit terms, because that is the base upon which we compete with other nations.

May 17, 1982
Export Development Act
The minister well understands the other difficulty. The euphemistic phrase used for it is "marketing expenses", but I think I have made my point that we in this House in all parties-I am sure the government party-will do everything we can to help the minister improve the performance of the Export Development Corporation, and the first step is getting a supply of capital at the lowest possible price so that we can compete with other nations doing the same thing. With a bigger bank roll we have some chance of success. I suggest that the principle of the Small Business Development Bond is a sound one. If the minister wants, other members of my party will explain other techniques.
The budget got rid of all these incentives to save money that were built up over the last seven or eight years, but they can be restored under this clause by allowing people to lend money to the Farm Credit Corporation. The income-averaging annuity could be used to spread income over a number of years. Retirement plans could be set up under this clause, or anything else you want. The only limitation is the initiative and the imagination of the staff administering it. If they are not already in the department, they should be hired, but this opportunity should not be missed. Any number of these devices could be used.
I put these things forward because as an ordinary Member of Parliament I am very pleased to see evidence of ideas that were presented in this House at the request of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and other ministers, put to use. A year ago we put forward some positive suggestions, and I am pleased to see them included in the budget and in this legislation. This proves that if one is patient and constant, sometimes one can manage to get certain items included in legislation.
In all humility, I say God bless the civil servant who sneaked this item into the bill. It gives the minister a chance to get around the budget which changed incentives into loopholes. It leaves room for cancelling the budget without loss of face.
The minister has an opportunity to let his imagination and initiative have free rein so that when the race is run he can say, "By jove, I got something done in spite of the system!" I should like to see the minister supported in that approach by all members of the House.
That is not the only way to get money, however. The minister must be aware that there is a lot of money around which is looking for investment. I am sure that officials in government are aware of this as well. I am referring particularly to Eurodollars and Petrodollars. The minister probably knows that there are people who are very anxious to get their money into the United States and into Canada. As far as I can establish it, if one were dealing with a Swiss bank today the effective rate would be about 11 per cent, and with Saudi Arabia it is probably about 10 per cent. Of course there is the risk of a change in value of the relative currencies when one borrows from such countries. There were some bad experiences seven years ago when a big change took place over a year and a half. However, these loans can be insured from any variation in the basic principal or in the rate of interest. A premium of 2 per cent is charged for this by most of the Swiss banks which
would bring it up to 13 per cent interest, but there would be no risk of a change in the value of the Canadian dollar.
I put that forward as the second alternative for getting cheaper money. Certainly the Export Development Corporation does not want to borrow money from the Consolidated Revenue Fund at 17 per cent. First of all, it is not available and second, who wants to pay 17 per cent when it can be borrowed at 11 per cent plus 2 per cent? The Arab investment corporations would probably charge about 10 per cent plus 2 per cent.
These things should be looked at by the minister. These people are desperate to get their money invested and also, they do not want it back too soon.
The same methods cannot be used in dealings with the developing nations. In those cases a three way trade operation is best. We cannot lend them money because they do not have a credit rating and it would be bad for them and bad for us. But a relationship could be set up through a well qualified international trading agency which knows that in order for these countries to pay us back, they would have to sell some of their goods somewhere else. The EDC is not equipped to do that-in fact none of our agencies are, but some private international trading companies do a good job with three way trade. The financing of such a deal becomes very complicated.
I am not trying to read the minister a lecture here but am simply pointing out some of the difficulties to him. Today, with our growing industrial might and our potential productivity growth, an export technique has to be developed at a very high level. It is important to get good terms on interest rates, the payout period and the marketing expense. These techniques are sometimes handled by an experienced international trading corporation.
Another thing to be negotiated is mutual advantage. The old North American concept in the days of economic imperialism was that there was only one type of deal-to get the best of it. The new type of deal that works with the more sophisticated developing nations is one that offers mutual advantage on both sides. This can always be arrived at if both parties approach it in the right spirit. Of course, every nation is different; in Mexico it is oil versus the CANDU. In Japan, it is whether they really want access to our resources in the future. It is important not to be backed down by Japanese politeness and firmness. As long as one speaks politely to the Japanese one can be tough. In fact, that is how they gain respect. With Europe it is also access to resources. If Europe wants our coal and our iron it will have to split its tariff structures. I am sure the minister knows how effective this idea is in dealing government to governent. In the case of Poland and the Iron Curtain countries the key is food. We have it, but the question is how they will get the money to pay for it. The minister knows the answer-it is three way trade. That is why I always put in my notes, "No more than three years' credit."
I will not speak of the joint enterprise technique and I will not speak of the international trade companies in detail nor
May 17, 1982

will I talk of the relative position of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund and so on.
I want to leave one thought with the House. This bill has given the minister an opportunity to put a credit base under the Export Development Corporation where he has a fighting chance to meet the competition from other industrialized nations engaged in the same business. It is a rough world out there. He has listened to my colleagues who have spoken of efficiency and how these things will be established, but I say that I wish the minister the best of luck in getting action immediately on this. We certainly need action immediately on our export business over the next few decades.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in support of this bill subject to the reservations expressed by my colleagues, which have been expressed for some very good reasons. This company is a wholly-owned Crown corporation with broad powers including the power to borrow, lend, guarantee loans, enter into export and foreign investment insurance contracts, and issue guarantees in respect of export transactions. Hopefully, some of the points raised by my colleagues will be fully dealt with in committee.
While the Export Development Corporation has been a useful instrument for expanding Canada's world trade, I think we all recognize that our record in international trade is not all that impressive. One can only speculate about what might have been had we not had the EDC. The record shows that Canada's share of world trade has declined over the last ten years from 4.9 per cent to 3 per cent. In absolute terms, and compared with other western industrialized nations, our productivity has declined rather dramatically and continues to do so. One only has to look at the recent budget papers, specifically the document entitled "Current Economic Situation" to see that Canada's productivity percentage change over the last ten years was 0.2 per cent. In the U.S. it was 0.6 per cent; in the U.K., 1.5 per cent; in Germany, 3.1 per cent; in France, 2.7 per cent; in Italy, 2.2 per cent; and in Japan, 3.4 per cent. So out of those seven countries, Canada has the worst record of performance. Our manufacturing sector can be described in general as being inefficient. I think it is fair to say we produce far too many lines, and our economies of scale are such that we find it difficult to compete in the international marketplace. We are weak in research and development, we do not have an effective marketing system, and we seem to lack a degree of persistence and continuity in exploiting and maintaining our markets. In other words, there is a tendency to be in and out of the marketplace; when things get a little tough, we withdraw; when we have a surplus we try to get involved in a marketing situation. So the in and out nature of our marketing strategy hinders us.
Excluding the auto pact trade, Canada's exports of fully manufactured goods represents only one fifth of our total exports, well below the average of one half to three fifths of all major industrial nations. This of course contributes to two of our very pressing problems, that of the balance of payments,
Export Development Act
and unemployment. In the 32-year period from 1950 to 1981, on only four different occasions did Canada manage to achieve a surplus in its current account. To a large extent it is fair to say that that has been caused by the outflow of dividends and the cost of servicing our debt, but our deficit in manufactured products during the 1970s was some $88 billion, $60 billion of that in the last five years of the decade.
That deficit is worsening, Mr. Speaker, when we look at the 1980s. In 1980-81 the manufacturing trade deficit was close to $40 billion, with no indication the trend is going to reverse. We rely far too much on our resource industries which are capital intensive and light in labour content. I am pleased that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is in the House today because he is grappling with the issue of railway capacity, particularly in western Canada. The demands on that capacity are largely in the natural resource sector, particularly coal, the west bound exports of which will increase from about 15 million tons in 1980 to about 59 million tons in 1990, an increase of about 350 per cent. Fertilizer components will increase by 78 per cent to 28 million tons, and raw forest products will increase by 65 per cent.
I guess, Mr. Speaker, that this is one of the arguments that western Canadian farmers placed before the minister, as they do before other politicians, when they say: we are being asked to share in the cost of increasing railway capacity, but what we are going to be doing is exporting a larger amount of our own real estate to other countries. That coal will probably come back to us in the form of a television set, refrigerator or automobile. On the other hand, the movement of grain will probably increase by maybe 40 per cent over the next ten years. So what we are doing in effect is aggravating the situation.
It is further aggravated by the fact that we are in a worldwide recession. The government continues to base its policy for economic recovery on resource megaprojects as outlined in the economic development strategy which accompanied the recent budget. That budget did nothing to enhance our manufacturing capability. As a matter of fact, it aggravates the situation as well, for example, the reduction in the capital cost allowance in the first year and the impact that has had on the automobile sector. In the leasing industry alone it will mean the loss of some 44,000 units during 1982. There are no incentives in the budget to encourage manufacturers to retool and improve their productivity. This whole question of reliance on resources and the failure to recognize our manufacturing potential is manifest in the fact we do not seem to have the resolve to increase our productivity, research and development, or to encourage retooling. These are all part of Canada's dismal performance record.
It is not very often that we have a bill of this nature to stimulate the kind of debate that I think has taken place here today. But when we really examine our own situation as a nation we find ourselves in a serious export crisis. I must

Export Development Act
compliment the agricultural sector, particularly the grain and oil seed sector. Once again I am pleased to see that the Minister of Transport is here. I think he has recognized the importance of the grain and oil seed sector, particularly the importance to Canada in terms of its export potential because it does generate huge amounts of spin-off activity. I know the minister addresses that problem most seriously. While we have slipped somewhat over the last ten years, we have not really penetrated our market potential in the way we should have. Perhaps that is due in part to the unreliability of our transportation system. I am happy to note, and I give full credit to the minister, that this year we will probably establish an all-time record of 26 million tonnes, which was the target established.
I have always been one to believe in establishment of targets. I did so when I was minister. I think you have to have something to strive for. 1 am pleased the minister and his colleague, the minister responsible for the Wheat Board, established a very ambitious target of 26 million metric tons, which I think will be achieved. It charges the system to work, to function, to iron out the wrinkles and the deficiencies.
Ten years ago we participated to the extent of 26 per cent of the world's wheat trade. Last year we recorded only about 17 per cent of the world's wheat trade. It means that while in aggregate terms Canada's share is going up, in terms of our penetration of markets Canada's share is going down. Clearly, that is a challenge to all of us. Part of that challenge is to improve our transportation system. We must also sharpen up our marketing abilities. I firmly believe that Canada's producers will produce if they are challenged with that task. The export of grain and oil seeds in Canada will generate some $5 billion to $6 billion in foreign exchange this year. When you look at the tremendous spin-off that is generated throughout the country, I think it fair to say that for every dollar's worth of export trade in grain and oil seed products, we witness a multiplier effect of something in the order of $4 to $5 which generates activity right across the country from Vancouver to the Atlantic sea ports. That is most remarkable. One only has to visit a place such as St. Catharines to recognize that that community is very much attached to and involved with the grain growing centres of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba. Notwithstanding the fact that there has been a dramatic increase in the price of imputs and a rather substantial reduction in the price of the net product to the producer, our producers are still competing in the international marketplace.
Take for example this year. When you look at the increase in input costs and couple that with the decline in prices in the international marketplace, you will note a 25 per cent reduction net income. Yet our producers are competing and penetrating that market. I merely make this point to indicate that given the will, the resources and the desire, we can compete and penetrate those international markets. I think the agriculture sector can be held up as a clear example of maintaining its prominence in ensuring we maintain the markets that have been established over the years. I hope we can improve. I am sure that we can improve because I believe our
May 17, 1982
trade potential in agricultural products is greater than what we have achieved to date.
I am not sure whether Canagrex will make any major impact on our ability to improve. The bill dealing with Canagrex at present is hung up in committee. I think there are some real second thoughts about the ability of Canagrex to achieve what it was intended to do. Whatever happens to Canagrex, given the right climate, given the right kind of transportation facilities and the marketing mechanism, and given the credit arrangements that are required, our agricultural producers can produce. There is no question about that.
One of the problems that affect Canada's ability to penetrate world markets is the arrangements in which we are involved with respect to GATT. Someone has suggested that as far as Canada is concerned we are the boy scouts in the trading world. Whether it is correct or whether it is implied, the fact still remains that we do not fare very well in terms of dealing with our counterparts in terms of how we honour commitments to GATT and how other countries, our competitors, get around some of these things. We recognize that there are protective shields which some countries adopt to protect their own sectors. We know there are tariffs; we know there are non-tariff barriers, we know there is a lot of unequal treatment, and we know dumping goes on.
1 have to point out that in the case of the megaprojects, and I refer to them once again, I think it is overlooked by many that out of the $440 billion worth of identified megaprojects, about 50 per cent relate to the electrical sector. When we look at what has happened in that sector we note that 10 per cent of those megaprojects are currently under way. We notice also that 80 per cent of the hardware for those megaprojects has been provided by offshore resources. While we are here talking about the need to penetrate our export market, we should also be talking about and recognizing the fact that we had better capture our own domestic markets. Dumping is crippling our basic manufacturing industry. That is clearly an area of government responsibility that should be addressed. There is no question that some nine hydro generator purchases in the last while have been supplied by offshore sources, essentially by Japan at 50 per cent below the prevailing price. These same markets are closed to foreign manufacturers. In other words, Canada cannot penetrate that market even if it wanted to.
As a matter of fact, when we look at specific prices, we note that in the case of one power transformer there was a differential of 35 per cent. That was the margin of dumping. In another case, the figure was 33 per cent. While we must stress the importance of export markets in penetrating markets and in achieving our potential, we have to make sure that our own market potential is not raped, that we have some protection for our own markets here in Canada.
In the area of agriculture and agricultural products, I am fully aware that the ECC and Japan have closed the door to many agricultural products, and agriculture is heavily subsidized. I could go on. I hope I will have the opportunity later on, either in committee or through further debate in this
May 17, 1982

House, to elaborate on some of the points that have to be made. I understand there is agreement to see that this bill moves on to committee. It is with that spirit of co-operation in the House that I will yield the floor. Speaking on behalf of our party, I believe, that we are prepared to see this bill move on to committee at this time.

subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR ADJUSTMENT INCREASE IN PENSIONS. (B) INQUIRY RESPECTING DATE OF PRESENTATION OF LEGISLATIVE AMENDMENTS
VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR ADJUSTMENT INCREASE IN PENSIONS. (B) INQUIRY RESPECTING DATE OF PRESENTATION OF LEGISLATIVE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight because of a totally unacceptable answer which I received from the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell) on May 12, 1982, to the question concerning increasing the basic rate of pension payment to disabled veterans. The minister's answer indicates to me that perhaps he has not done his homework as well as he might have. I asked the minister how he could justify allowing some 130,000 veterans to fall $900 behind the composite group of the public service in terms of pension payment. Also I asked the minister to introduce amendments to Section 58 of the Pension Act which would provide that pension increases reflect the principle of parity with the average wage of five unskilled categories of public servants or the increase in the consumer price index, whichever is greater, and that this principle be entrenched in the Pension Act. Such an amendment would guarantee veterans a fair and constant increase compared with increases in the public service.
The minister replied that he had not enough time to study the proposal which had been presented through my question and by national veterans' organizations of Canada in the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. The minister failed to realize in this admission that this very same recommendation had been put forward by veterans' organizations, by various governmental committees and by a 1972 study group established by and with representation from his own departmental officials. As far back as 1972, his department was recommending that, and I quote from the study group recommendations:
Adjournment Debate
It would seem readily apparent to the study group that these disabled veterans should be permitted to join in the standard of living available to other Canadians, and should not be restricted to relating future increases in pension to the cost of living today. By their service and sacrifice they have earned the right to enjoy the standards which working Canadians have as a matter of course.
The recommendations of the study group continued:
Pensions should be adjusted annually on a fixed day in accordance with changes in the average wage rates for the public service groups selected and taking into account income tax deductions in effect on that fixed date.
If the minister and his department need more than ten years to study and implement such a simple amendment to the Pension Act, it is no wonder that more complicated problems like pension application processing delays have been with us since the advent of the veterans' benefits system. Ten years is simply too long for any person to have to wait for a simple decision, yet the minister says that he needs more time to review the proposal. Meanwhile, veterans' organizations must come hat in hand to plead on behalf of their members for pension increases on a yearly basis just so veterans can survive.
There have been a number of encouraging improvements made to the management and operation levels of the department, but there is no reason this healthy trend should not continue here tonight by the minister agreeing to the cancellation of this grovelling which veterans must do just to keep up with the cost of living.
I am especially pleased that the minister recently stated in the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs that he had no objection to a six-month time limit on pension processing and the appeal process, except for the possibility that the retrieval of medical records would be hard to accomplish. Surely, with the introduction of the computer system on which the department's newspaper has reported so glowingly, the retrieval of medical documentation from one end of the country to the other will be accomplished well within three months, thus leaving three months for appeal procedures.
In response to my questions tonight, I know the minister will reply that it has only been recently that veterans have actually fallen behind. Still, he cannot justify making them come back year after year to beg for increases just to keep up with the cost of living. This is a completely unnecessary complication both for veterans' organizations and for the department. If it is true that such amendments would not cost the department unaffordable sums of money, what sense does it make not to have the system regularized by having annual automatic increases?
The amendment to the Pension Act which has now been recommended by almost every veterans' association in Canada, by the Senate Committee on Health, Welfare and Science, by officials within the Department of Veterans Affairs, and by the Conservative Party can no longer be ignored on the basis that it is under review. I hope the minister will stand up tonight to accede to the many proponents of this proposal and that he will tell us that legislation will be forthcoming before the summer recess. He could be sure of all-party support and quick passage if this were the case. Disabled veterans across Canada will be very interested in the minister's reply tonight.

May 17, 1982
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Hon. W. Bennett Campbell (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR ADJUSTMENT INCREASE IN PENSIONS. (B) INQUIRY RESPECTING DATE OF PRESENTATION OF LEGISLATIVE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, in 1973 the basic rate of disability pension was set so that a pensioner without dependants, whose disability or disabilities were assessed at 100 per cent, would receive a pension equivalent to the composite average salary of five selected categories of unskilled public servants, after income tax had been deducted, as if the public servant lived in the province with the lowest tax rate. Of course, we all realize that income tax is not payable on pensions paid by the Canadian Pension Commission.
As of January 1, 1982, the average annual salary of the five categories of public servants was $10,371. This meant that there was a difference of $554.52 per annum between the average annual salary after taxes in favour of the 100 per cent unmarried disability pensioner who receives $10,925.52 per annum following a 12.2 per cent increase, in line with the consumer price index.
Following recent wage adjustments in certain of the civil service categories used in computing the composite average salary, as of April 1, 1982, the salary after tax of the average of the five selected categories of single public servants is $988.91 a month, or $11,867 per annum, while a 100 per cent unmarried disability pensioner receives $910.46 per month, or $10,925.52 per annum, for a difference of $78.45 per month or $941.48 per year in favour of the composite public servant. A married 100 per cent disability pensioner with no dependent children receives $13,656.96 per annum, whereas the married average public servant will receive $12,613.00 per year after tax for a difference of $1,043.96 per annum in favour of the disability pensioner.
It should be noted that approximately 76 per cent of disability pensioners are married, and therefore most pensioners receive substantially more than the composite public servant who, as we all realize, receives nothing extra for being married.
The Royal Canadian Legion and the National Council of Veteran Associations have indicated their concern with the present rate of pension, and I wish to assure hon. members that I have this subject under very active consideration.

subtopic: THE ECONOMY-LEVEL OF INTEREST RATES. (B) REQUEST THAT NEW BUDGET BE INTRODUCED
THE ECONOMY-LEVEL OF INTEREST RATES. (B) REQUEST THAT NEW BUDGET BE INTRODUCED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday last, I raised a question with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) because of the change of interest rates in Canada on Thursday. Your Honour will recall that interest rates in Canada rose a quarter of 1 per cent, or 25 basis points, on Thursday. At the same time, interest rates in the United States declined 40 basis points, increasing the separation between Canadian and American interest rates to very close to 3 per cent per annum.
Your Honour will recall that the government has blamed the Americans for our interest rate problems in Canada, but the fact is that the basis of the treasury bills is that interest rates in Canada are very close to 3 per cent above those in the
United States. Commercial paper is about 2 per cent above that in the United States, and it is a little better than that on long-term Canada bonds. The effect is that we have a high interest rate policy in this country. We presumably have it to maintain the value of the Canadian dollar. The Prime Minister was concerned that I was trying to advocate a lower dollar, in his opinion. That is not the case. The Prime Minister knew perfectly that we had 35 hours of debate the previous week with respect to the economic problems of this country, initiated because of the failure of the Alsands project. In that debate we made a number of references to what needs to be done in this country to turn around the economic conditions of Canada and reduce interest rates.
We have said time and again that the budget of November 12 must be dumped. It has almost been dumped, but it has to go completely in order to cut down the uncertainty and lack of confidence in Canada.
We said that we have to reverse the National Energy Program which has driven capital out of the country. In fact, lately there has been a flood of capital out of the country. In order to balance that capital, we have to pay higher and higher interest rates in order to attract hot money from the rest of the world to this country.
We said that we must take a very serious look at the Foreign Investment Review Agency. The government refuses to do that. It brings in legislation that discriminates against foreign capital. It gives Canadians generally the attitude that their capital might be expropriated.
We have said to the government it must change its penchant for creating a series of grant and loan programs. We have almost a Campbell's alphabet soup of initials for various programs, enterprise development-oriented programs, housing programs, or whatever. We have a whole series of programs involved in grants which Canadians are supposed to look at as a benefit from government. We said that should be reversed. Instead, we should have incentives in the tax system to encourage Canadians to invest and make Canada a place where they can stand and grow.
We have told the Prime Minister time and again that if he really wanted to make this country grow, he would look seriously at the capital gains tax structure in this country. If he did that, he would see that most of the capital gains tax the government collects is as a result of inflation. True gains should be indexed. In fact, we would be better off without the whole concept.
Time and again we have said the government should get its costs under control. It must reduce government overhead to below the rate of inflation, not above as it has been for the last year, this year 16'/2 per cent of the budget and 22 per cent the year before, far above the rate of inflation. Time and again we have said it must control costs, but the government has yet to do that.
May 17, 1982

We have said time after time that the government should look at the various departments of government and at such things as Consolidated Computers. We spoke tonight about the Enterprise Development Corporation and corporations such as Canadair which have benefited from all sorts of loans, grants and programs. Money is funded into unprofitable and very marginally profitable operations at enormous costs. The Prime Minister refuses to look at these. No wonder the Canadian dollar drops. No wonder interest rates go up higher and higher in Canada. This government refuses to look at remedies proposed by the opposition and by Canadians generally. With blinders on, it continues its high interest rate policy designed to ensure that our recession will become a massive depression.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: THE ECONOMY-LEVEL OF INTEREST RATES. (B) REQUEST THAT NEW BUDGET BE INTRODUCED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am surprised to hear such a hodge-podge of fuzzy economic thinking from the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) who usually presents himself as knowledgeable on economic matters. He approached an important topic, the question of interest rates and inflation in Canada. He presented a long list of what he sees as sins by the government as the cause for high interest rates. I am surprised that in the list of those sins he did not give even a token acknowledgement of the fact that he was acting as a spokesman for a very reasonably small group of privileged people. He was attacking some very important programs that happened to help a broad spectrum of business, industry, labour and ordinary people in this country.
The hon. member's claim that we can drop interest rates is a direct lead-in to several important economic consequences. He does not want to tell us that his claim to drop interest rates will lead to a devalued dollar, that it will push up prices enormously for ordinary Canadians. He does not want to tell us that this higher inflation, which will result from his policies, will end up eroding the savings of ordinary people, especially the pensioners in his riding who depend very much on their savings. He does not want to tell us that the kind of thinking he has given us leads to the sort of panic and despondency, the kind of bad psychology, that he wants to lay at the government's door.
These are the logical consequences of the kind of attack and the kind of policies that he has presented. I am surprised to hear him make the claim that we can arbitrarily drop interest rates. It sounds to me that once again the hon. member is cozying up with the NDP and its kind of magical economic thinking. Usually he tries to present himself as something more Conservative than that. He knows full well that the real way to get rid of high interest rates is threefold. First, it is for all of us to dedicate ourselves to some kind of fight against inflation, some kind of restraint that will get inflation down. Second, we need to encourage areas of genuine growth, genuine strength. Third, we need in the course of this activity to find the people who are suffering from the recession and to provide them with specific and well-deserved help to help them bridge these difficult times. That is what this government is involved in,

Mr. Speaker. We are not involved in negative thinking, negative attack or magical answers.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT-VOLUNTARY AFFIRMATIVE ACTION PROGRAM-REPORTED CONTENTS OF MEMORANDUM. (B) REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF MANDATORY PROGRAM
EMPLOYMENT-VOLUNTARY AFFIRMATIVE ACTION PROGRAM-REPORTED CONTENTS OF MEMORANDUM. (B) REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF MANDATORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I rise this evening because the response to the question that I put to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) on May 14 of this year was totally inadequate. My question was with regard to the affirmative action program, and I want to spend a couple of minutes indicating why that question was important.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that basically what we are dealing with here is a program that attempts to help disadvantaged people, native people, women, and the handicapped. The facts that lead to the creation of such a program are that, for example, 60 per cent of all women in the labour force end up working in jobs which are classified as clerical, sales or service. There is nothing wrong with these jobs in and of themselves, but when 60 per cent of all women work in these kinds of jobs only, rather than in senior management, for example, or in professional employment, these jobs in themselves become job ghettoes. These low-paying jobs, dead-end jobs, mean that women today earn only 60 per cent of what men earn. That is, for every dollar that a man earns, a woman who is working full time will be earning 60 cents.
The reason that I asked the question with regard to affirmative action is that affirmative action in other jurisdictions has proven to be a good, effective way to bring about greater equality in the incomes and working conditions of men and women.
In my question to the minister I began by focusing upon Manitoba in which over a period of seven years of a supposed affirmative action program, no agreement has been signed between the government and the private sector to establish these affirmative action programs. The fact that there has been no agreement has been well known to everybody, including the minister, and therefore was clear evidence that nothing was happening in the area of affirmative action, that there were no results coming out of the government's activity. To underline the fact that the government was not getting any results, a memo came to public light over the last week or so. I would like to quote from that memo directed to affirmative action consultants, those civil servants whose job it is to go out into the community to meet with companies in the private sector to encourage them to establish affirmative action programs. These consultants received the following directions in a written memo:
-you will not promote Affirmative Action nor visit employers in this regard. In addition, you will not conduct any seminars or disseminate any information to the field to explain or promote Affirmative Action.
That memo in and of itself is shocking and disgraceful, and I must say it was not surprising that when this came to the

May 17, 1982
Adjournment Debate
attention of the minister, he ordered an investigation. I have only one comment about the investigation, which the minister describes as a full investigation: the investigation is an internal departmental investigation. I think the public would have more confidence in this investigation if it were a public, open investigation in which everyone could see that justice were done rather than being an internal departmental investigation, in other words, the department investigating itself.
However, be that as it may, there is an investigation, and perhaps some good will come of it. I certainly hope it does because if there is any way to put a little energy behind the affirmative action program in Manitoba, perhaps it will be found in that investigation.
What strikes me most deeply about the memo is the fact that it raises the whole question of what level of commitment to affirmative action the government has. Just how much energy is the government putting into affirmative action? The memo raises this question because it seems to me that only in government which has no real and firm commitment to an affirmative action program could any civil servant even conceive of writing such a memo to employees whose job or mandate it is to promote such a program. I think what the government has to deal with is the whole question of its level of commitment to affirmative action.
The minister responded to me by saying that the government is deeply committed to affirmative action and citing the "very major" success of the affirmative action program in the public sector. I want to put on the record a few facts about the program in the public sector, which the minister describes as a very major success and as evidence that the government is deeply committed to affirmative action. The annual report of the Public Service Commission for 1981 gives statistics in relation to affirmative action in the public sector, and I will put some of those on the record here tonight. Only 4.3 per cent of the management category in the public service are women, and 81.6 per cent of the administrative support category are women, so at the top end of the public service there are mostly men and at the bottom end of the public service there are mostly women. With regard to salary levels, 67 per cent of public servants earning less than $10,000 were women, while 97 per cent of those earning over $50,000 were men.
I see an indication that I should be winding up very quickly.
I just want to say that the statistics I have quoted-and many more could be quoted-demonstrate that the results of affirmative action are as bleak in the public service as they are in the private sector.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT-VOLUNTARY AFFIRMATIVE ACTION PROGRAM-REPORTED CONTENTS OF MEMORANDUM. (B) REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF MANDATORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before discussing the specific question let me provide for the
hon. member some background information about the affirmative action program.
Affirmative action is a process undertaken by an employer to identify and eliminate systematic discrimination and to redress the imbalances in the work force caused by past discrimination. Affirmative action was first enunciated as commission policy in 1979 and became operational in the 1979-80 fiscal year.
There are presently 16 affirmative action consultants located in the major centres across the country. For example, there are two such affirmative action consultants in Winnipeg. It is true that affirmative action has not enjoyed a great deal of success in signing agreements with employers in the past few years. Many employers have a negative perception of affirmative action based upon the American experience. Some employers, in addition, fear that by signing an agreement they will be admitting that there is presently something wrong with their hiring practices. This attitude neither helps the employer nor target group members who are being excluded from jobs. Finally, there is a group of employers who simply feel that any government intervention in business is unacceptable. For these and many other reasons, affirmative action has had a difficult introductory period.
The hon. member has asked if we should not now consider a mandatory affirmative action program utilizing the contract compliance mechanism. In response, let me say that the minister is not happy with the voluntary program because it does not seem to meet the needs of disadvantaged workers nor the needs of the employer community. He is, therefore, determined to make changes in the approach being used, and it is for this reason that they are presently reviewing the affirmative action strategy and are considering various options. They will, of course, continue to consult with business and labour before taking a final decision in order to ensure that any new policy option will be workable.
With regard to the specific situation which has risen in Manitoba, the minister has now seen the memos. Mr. Lussier, Chairman of the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission has been asked to investigate the situation and to provide the minister with a detailed report at the earliest possible time. If, in fact, the report shows that our officials were operating contrary to commission policy, the situation will be immediately rectified.
